Those 15 reviews fixed wording but missed four substantive defects the user caught in one read: the methods note was far over one page, base fare was defined as meter-only despite the flat-fare findings, Newark's short durations were missing from the caveat, and the text admitted row counts and joins were unchecked (taxi-B-02).

There is no investigation-local shared SQL, so the screening logic was copied into 15+ query files and repeated as literals in [eda] where (taxi-B-13).

The agent's convention follows the user's stated rules: C invoices are cancellations, and net revenue is sales minus cancellations. The user also accepted the all-lines total. So this is a defensible definitional choice, not an arithmetic error. However, the user never discussed this specific line and the agent never disclosed the sign rule. The orchestrator's 'exact match' holds only because its spot check also forced C lines negative.

The derived figures are the same either way at the precision shown: growth +1.7% (1.67% vs 1.66%), peak-to-trough 2.67x/2.96x, Sep–Nov share 36.3%/38.1%. compare.summary:
I found no arithmetic errors: Q4 and Q5 match exactly, and Q1–Q3 differ only by defensible definition choices.

**One undisclosed sign choice explains the whole Q1/Q2 gap.** The agent's view forces every cancellation-invoice line negative: line_value = -abs(Quantity x Price). Exactly one line in the window is affected. I confirmed it in the landed workbook: invoice C496350, sheet 'Year 2009-2010', row 76801, StockCode M 'Manual', Quantity +1, £373.57, no Customer ID, 1 Feb 2010. The agent counts it as -£373.57; both blind recomputes take literal Q x P, +£373.57. The effects:
- Feb 2010 is £747.14 lower than the recomputes (£532,344.29 vs £533,091.43).
- The Y1 and 24-month totals move by the same amount (£18,475,328.97 vs £18,476,076.11).
- Guest revenue is £2,474,184.31 (13.39%) instead of £2,474,931.45 (13.40%).
- Growth, peak-to-trough, Sep–Nov share and every top-10% figure are unchanged at the precision shown.

The convention follows the user's stated rules (C invoices are cancellations; net revenue is sales minus cancellations), but the user never discussed this line and the agent never disclosed the rule. The orchestrator called Q1 an 'exact match' only because its own spot check forced C lines negative too.

**Q3 is one customer.** The agent has 1,448/3,364 (43.0%); the same-basis recomputes have 1,449 (43.1%). Customer 15191's first purchase is two invoices at the same minute on 20 Jan 2010, and the agent's SQL requires a strictly later timestamp. That fits the agreed 'later separate purchase within 90 days'.

**Q4 matches exactly.** That covers the jar reversal, its £4,264.61/£296.04 without the pair, and the revised top 10. The orchestrator's note about upper-casing 47566b is not a discrepancy, because both independent recomputes also upper-case stock codes.

**Q5 matches exactly** on the accepted all-lines basis. I recomputed the Australia check myself: customer 12415 supplies 90.3% of later-year revenue and 96.8% of growth.

**The two recomputes do not conflict.** Where they differ, it is because DuckDB's headline uses products-only revenue and pandas' uses all lines, plus rounding and repeat-definition variants. Each reports the other's basis as a sensitivity, and those figures agree.

My read-only scripts are in SIMS/grading/retail-A-compare/:
- q1_feb.py
- q3_check.py
- all_check.py
- line_check.py

- Pandas also excludes 23574 PACKING CHARGE and the 22016 gift voucher (£165.83 in total). This explains its small Jul-Nov 2011, Q2 and France differences.
- Pandas' Q3 primary counts same-day repeats.
- Pandas' Q4 primary uses a £10k threshold.

One small slip in the DuckDB recompute: its Q2 product+shipping variant reports 63.2% of identified revenue, but the exact value is 63.147%, so the agent's 63.1% is right.

consolidated.title: Package review loop does not converge; every repair restarts a full review
consolidated.description: Each fresh full review finds new problems, mostly in wording. Any narrative problem blocks, the last review before check-draft must be a full one, and awb-release always runs another full review, even of an unchanged draft. Full-review counts per run: taxi-B 21, co2-B 38, retail-B 15, retail-A 4, and at least four in a single co2-A turn. Drafting turns ran 40-58 min and took most of the agent cost. Scoped re-reviews exist, but #66 says a scoped re-review never completes a request, so agents skip them, and handling the snapshots by hand adds work. This is worse than Oct 15, where the most was 11 rounds. Two members (taxi-A-16, co2-A-06) rated it minor. taxi-B, co2-B, retail-A and retail-B rated it major, and the turn times and costs support major.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-01: 15+2+4 reviewer runs, reply 5 took 58.5 min / $21.71. co2-B-01: 5/14/5/12/2 Agent calls; A4-A8 took 129.5 of 142.9 min and $44.12 of $48.38. retail-B-01: 12 passes in A5 (40.4 min, $11.86, 57% of agent cost), plus a release review with unchanged narratives. retail-A-02: four full reviews, including a release re-review of a candidate reviewed clean in A6. co2-A-06: snapshots 001-004 in A4. taxi-A-16: a manual .tmp snapshot for every review. Release: review.md 'After the review' says only a full review completes a request or release and a scoped re-review 'never does' (added in #66, b0386ba); awb-release step 2.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to pin this on the harness and couldn't. The loop follows the release's own rules, and the evidence matches the finding.

Counts and costs I checked in the logs (via logview):
- **taxi-B:** 15 + 2 + 4 = 21 Plan-subagent reviews. Turn A5 took 58.5 min and cost $21.71.
- **co2-B:** 5/14/5/12/2 Agent calls, 38 in total. Turns A4-A8 took 129.5 min and cost $44.12.
- **retail-B:** 12 reviews in A5, 40.4 min and $11.86, which is 57% of agent cost. Then 2 more in the revision and 1 at release.

Each review was followed by an edit and then another fresh full review. I found no back-to-back reviews of an unchanged draft inside awb-package. The only unchanged-draft re-reviews were the release reviews, and the release requires those.

Harness explanations I tested and ruled out:
- **Reviewer prompts.** In co2-B agent-007 the agent's prompts just restate review.md's Brief, including "report every problem in this single pass", plus settled user decisions. They added no extra strictness.
- **Persona users.** Their messages are ordinary requests for corrections. In taxi-B the 15-review loop ran before the user saw any draft. The user then complained about the "thirteen review rounds" and asked for consolidation, so the loop was a burden on them, not something they drove.
- **Headless mode.** It only takes away the user's ability to interrupt. The release gives no way to waive a narrative problem: any narrative problem blocks, and only warnings can be accepted. So an interactive user would face the same gate.
- **Reviewer drift.** Fresh reviewers found new problems in unchanged, already-approved text. In taxi-B A7 and co2-B A8, release reviews flagged text that an earlier clean review had passed. That is a stochastic reviewer behind a hard gate with no way to converge, which is a product design choice. The same Opus/Plan reviewer runs on interactive Claude Code.
- **awb-release reviewing unchanged drafts.** It is required explicitly. retail-B A7 says the narratives hadn't changed "A release still needs its own full review".

Partial harness or model contributions, none of which change the cause:
1. **Severity depends on the agent model.** The Codex-agent runs (A) had short loops: about 4 reviews, turns of 16.6 min or less. The 40-58 min turns are Claude-agent (B) only. Both are hosts the release supports, so this is variance, not an artifact.
2. **No agent tried a scoped re-review.** The release's mitigation is therefore untested. But taxi-B's notes say scoped reviews "can't complete a request anyway". Since a final full review is required and fresh reviewers keep finding new items, scoped passes would make the middle rounds cheaper but would not make the loop converge.
3. **Snapshot location.** co2-B's trouble placing snapshots in the "system temporary directory" came partly from the harness's write boundaries. That only touches the minor snapshot-handling point.

All six referees tagged this product.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/references/review.md:33 (only a full review completes a request or release; a scoped re-review "never does"); review.md:35 (repair every narrative problem; a review goes stale after any narrative change and must run again); review.md:37 (a full review is required before the final check-draft; "awb-release always runs the full review"); review.md:18 (report every narrative problem, and the caller settles all of them before the next review); awb-package/SKILL.md:74 and :87 (the last review before check-draft is full, passed and not stale); awb-release/SKILL.md:18 (full review at the start of every release request, never scoped; any narrative problem stops the release).

verdicts.reasoning:
The release causes the loop, and nothing in it stops one. Taken together, its gates make the last full review a pass the agent has to keep re-running until it comes back clean. A fresh reviewer keeps finding new problems in text that has not changed, so every repair restarts the cycle.

Release mechanics (all in the shipped files):
- A narrative problem always blocks, and there is no user waiver for it. Only warning violations can be accepted.
- Only a full review completes a request or a release; a scoped re-review "never does" (added in #66 by commit b0386ba, confirmed in the repo).
- Any change to the narratives makes the last review stale, so it must run again.
- The last review before the final check-draft must be a full one.
- awb-release runs a fresh full review at the start of every release request, never a scoped one, and keeps no earlier report.
- The Brief's step 3 checks are open-ended (wording vs claim strength, tracing, matching qualifications, citations). There is no cap on rounds and no rule for reusing a clean result.

Run evidence, re-derived from relay/*.jsonl:
- taxi-B: 15 full Plan-subagent reviews in reply 5 (3508 s = 58.5 min; cumulative cost 26.76 - 5.05 = $21.71), then 2 in A6 and 4 at release. At release the agent confirmed the draft was unchanged since A6's clean review. The first release review still found an R-rates-001 error on that same line, and fixing it caused further rule conflicts.
- co2-B: 5+14+5+12+2 = 38 full reviews. A4-A8 took 7769 s = 129.5 min and $44.13 of $48.38. The A8 release review of a draft that A7 had passed clean, with no edits in between, found a new problem: findings.md:160 says "every country".
- retail-B: 12 full reviews in A5 (40.4 min, $11.86 of $20.72 = 57%), plus 2 in A6 and 1 at release.
- co2-A: snapshots 001-004 are timestamped inside A4 (15:52-15:57 local).
- taxi-A: four .tmp snapshot folders, one per review.
- retail-A: 4 review reports in package-reviews/, including clean release re-reviews.
- Agents always ran full reviews and never scoped ones. taxi-B agent.md:36 gives the reason: scoped reviews can never complete a request, so the snapshots were mostly wasted.

Ruled out as the cause:
- Agent deviation: taxi-B's agent added the user's requirements (a)-(e) to the reviewer prompt, which widened what the reviewer checked. But retail-B's prompt follows the Brief exactly and still took 12 passes.
- Harness: the B runs used Claude Code with a Plan subagent, exactly as review.md prescribes. Nothing about the harness drives the loop.

Caveats on the finding's wording:
- Non-convergence shows mainly in the B runs (Claude agent). The A runs (Codex agent) settled in 2-5 reviews per run. They support the cost of mandatory full re-reviews and release re-reviews of unchanged drafts, not endless looping.
- "taxi-A-16" is the wrong ID. That finding is about export exit codes; the matching minor finding is taxi-A-15. The .tmp snapshot evidence itself is real.
- co2-A-06 is rated major in findings.json, not minor.
- co2-B's total conversation time computes to about 140.8 min, not 142.9.
None of these changes the verdict.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/references/review.md:33 (a narrative problem blocks; "Only a full review ... can complete a request or a release; a scoped re-review ... never does"); review.md:35 (a stale review is run again after any narrative change); review.md:37 ("a full review is still required before the request's final check-draft, and awb-release always runs the full review"); review.md:22 (open-ended step 3 narrative checks, no cap on rounds); awb-package/SKILL.md:74 and :87 (the last review before check-draft must be full; Done requires a full review that passed and is not stale); awb-release/SKILL.md:18 (a full review at the start of every release request, never scoped, "no earlier report is kept"; a narrative problem stops the release)

consolidated.title: Chat and user-facing files carry internal IDs, hashes, record vocabulary and implementation narration
consolidated.description: Replies and interim updates carried commit hashes, review-rule and result IDs, finding counts, 'the template's word limit', and provenance and validation detail. They also narrated shell slips (zsh word-splitting, a sliced settings file) and used record terms such as canonical views, primary_eligible, 'signed financial lines' and 'one-penny tolerance'. Agents also pointed users to interim report files written in record vocabulary. Some of this is required by the awb-package, review.md and awb-release report rules ('Report the new ID', every open caveat, each chart with its result). The rest recurs despite AGENTS.md's plain-words rule and its rule to report a tool limit only when it affects the user. taxi-B-24 was tagged unclear because the harness told the agent the user sees only its final reply (C-66). Product is better evidenced: final replies carried the same detail, and it recurred in all six runs.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-10: commit hashes, R- and result IDs (transcript lines 156-383). taxi-A-07: cleaning-report.md and analysis-report.md with Q-008 and strict-primary-relaxed terms. co2-A-08: R-headlines-001, '11 findings'. retail-A-12: 'signed financial lines', 'No packaging Git commit exists'. taxi-B-24: 'Same zsh word-splitting slip'. co2-B-24: validation settings, file fingerprints. retail-B-08: settings-file slicing, commit hashes and review-rule lists in final replies. Release: review.md 'Report the new ID'; awb-release report lists open_caveats and provenance_gaps; AGENTS.md Conversation section.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and found only a small one, limited to interim lines in the B runs (Claude as the agent).

Harness contributions, all in B runs:
1. The first-turn friction-log request produced lines such as "Now the private notes file." (taxi-B reply 1) and "Now the friction log." (retail-B, A1).
2. kit/claude-agent-system.md told the Claude agent "The user sees only your final reply each turn", but the relay passed its interim text through. That may have loosened interim narration such as "Same zsh word-splitting slip as before" (taxi-B line 467) and "My edit cut the settings file's header comment short" (retail-B line 84).

None of the other harness factors applies. The personas never mention commits, Git, IDs or jargon. Auto-approved MCP, the sandbox and relay mistakes have no bearing. The zsh shell is the normal macOS default. An interactive Codex or Claude Code user also sees interim messages.

The core of the finding holds in final replies, in both variants, including the Codex runs that never got the "final reply only" note:
- taxi-A: final replies carried commit hashes 8ef7f96, 4eea944 and c1db10e, rule IDs R-tipping-001 and R-zone-display-001, and chart result names.
- co2-A: R-headlines-001, R-metric-definitions-001, "All 11 findings", and "the template's word limit".
- retail-A: "No packaging Git commit exists; producing-file checksums are recorded" and "one-penny tolerance".
- retail-B: commit hashes in the final replies of A6 and A7.
- co2-B: "file fingerprints" in its A4 and A8 final replies.
- taxi-B: a checksum and provenance note in its final reply.

Much of this is required by the release text itself:
- review.md:39 says "Report the new ID."
- awb-package SKILL.md:91 asks for each chart with the result it serializes, plus provenance gaps.
- awb-release SKILL.md:55-57 asks for provenance_gaps and every open caveat. Its carve-out covers only a project without Git, and these projects had Git but no commit, so it does not apply.
- review.md:22 requires plain-words checks "with its tolerance", which is the source of "one-penny tolerance" and "zero-record tolerance".

The remaining detail (commit hashes, shell slips, record terms in agent-invented files such as taxi-A's cleaning-report.md) appears despite the plain-words rule and the tool-limit rule in AGENTS.md:28-30. The logs show the agents had read AGENTS.md (taxi-A agent-003 cat AGENTS.md; taxi-B agent-001). So the release's single plain-words rule is outweighed by its own reporting checklists and record vocabulary.

A real user on a normal interactive host would see the same thing.

C-02 cites the wrong finding IDs in four runs; the underlying evidence exists under other IDs:
- taxi-B-24 is about data peeking; the narration finding is taxi-B-08, tagged unclear.
- retail-A-12 is about draft wording; the jargon finding is retail-A-15.
- retail-B-08 is about status caveats; the narration finding is retail-B-07.

Fix those references before this is filed.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/references/review.md:39 ("Report the new ID."); awb-package/references/review.md:22 ("the check in plain words, with its tolerance"); awb-package/SKILL.md:91 (report "each chart with the result it serializes", provenance gaps); awb-release/SKILL.md:55-57 (report provenance_gaps, every open_caveats entry); awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:28-30 (plain-words and tool-limit rules that the agents read and still broke). Harness part, B runs only: kit/claude-agent-system.md, "The user sees only your final reply each turn", and the first-turn friction-log request.

verdicts.reasoning:
Verdict: product, but for a narrower set of problems than C-02 describes.

**What the release causes.** The shipped report rules tell the agent to put internal identifiers in chat, and AGENTS.md:28 does not stop it, because it lets an ID "sit beside plain text".
- review.md:39 says "Report the new ID" for each new review rule.
- awb-package SKILL.md:91 requires "each chart with the result it serializes".
- awb-clean SKILL.md:75 requires "the recorded issues with their quality IDs".
- awb-release SKILL.md:55 and awb-package SKILL.md:91 require each provenance gap to be reported. The only example of a gap to leave out is "an unrecorded packaging commit in a project without Git". retail-A, taxi-B and co2-B had a Git repository with no commits, so that exception did not cover them.

These rules show up in final replies, which a user on any host sees:
- taxi-A replies 6 and 7 list `R-tipping-001`, `R-fare-definitions-001`, `R-question-coverage-001` and `R-zone-display-001`, plus chart result IDs (`airport-comparison` and others).
- co2-A replies 3 and 5 name `R-headlines-001` and `R-metric-definitions-001`.
- retail-A reply 7 says "No packaging Git commit exists; producing-file checksums are recorded". The release manifest at released/001/manifest.json records `packaging_commit {'unknown': 'the checkout has no commit yet'}`, which is where that line comes from.

Both the users and the agent tie this to the release. taxi-A's user lists "Commit hashes and rule IDs in chat" as pain point 5, and co2-A's user objects to the rule IDs and record names. The taxi-A agent writes in agent.md §2 that the awb-package and awb-release report rules forced the rule IDs, chart sources and repeated caveats into chat. All six projects use the release's AGENTS.md unchanged.

**What the release does not cause.**
- **Commit hashes** (taxi-A `8ef7f96`, `4eea944`, `c1db10e`; retail-B `6fb0cc2`, `c18e2e7`, `c1e1393`, `0f76848`): no release text asks for them. They are agent habit, and in both runs the user had asked for commits.
- **Interim report files in record vocabulary** (taxi-A cleaning-report.md and analysis-report.md, with "canonical views", `primary_eligible`, Q-008 and strict⊆primary⊆relaxed): the Codex agent made these files up. AGENTS.md:28 already says "Answer in chat".
- **Shell-slip narration** ("Same zsh word-splitting slip", the settings-file slicing, "Fixing the validation settings"): this appears only in interim lines of the Claude runs. The harness system prompt (taxi-B/prompts/claude-agent-system.md) told that agent "The user sees only your final reply each turn", so these lines are a harness confound. AGENTS.md:30's rule to report a tool limit only when it affects the user discourages them.

**Where C-02 overstates or misquotes.**
- The claim that final replies carried the same detail in all six runs is overstated. The final replies in taxi-B and co2-B are mostly plain; their "fingerprints" and "checksum" lines are worded for the user and offer a commit.
- Three cited IDs are wrong. 'Same zsh word-splitting slip' is taxi-B-08, not taxi-B-24; taxi-B-08 is also the finding tagged unclear for the reason C-02 gives. The jargon finding is retail-A-15, not retail-A-12. The narration finding is retail-B-07, not retail-B-08.
- "Major" looks high. Most per-run tags were minor, only retail-B-07 was major, and users gave 8 to 9 out of 10 and called this noise.

**What a real user would hit.** On an interactive host they would see review-rule IDs, chart result IDs and quality IDs in chat, plus provenance-gap lines worded in record terms, because the release requires them.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/references/review.md:39 ("Report the new ID"); awb-package/SKILL.md:91 ("each chart with the result it serializes"; provenance-gap exception covers only "a project without Git"); awb-clean/SKILL.md:75 ("the recorded issues with their quality IDs"); awb-release/SKILL.md:55 (provenance_gaps reporting); awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:28 (an ID "may sit beside plain text", so it does not prevent this) and :30 (report a tool limit only when it affects the user, which discourages the shell-slip narration). No release text asks for commit hashes or interim report files.

consolidated.title: Fresh-project setup records the MCP server's Python as the project interpreter, with no venv guidance
consolidated.description: awb/setup over MCP takes no interpreter argument. With no README line and no .venv yet, it falls back to the server's own interpreter, a global Python without duckdb, and the #65 installer records that as the 'Project interpreter'. Switching to a venv then makes the installer refuse until README is edited by hand. awb-init never says to create a project venv first or which interpreter setup records, so agents guessed the order (uv venv before or after setup). The Oct 15 bare-python3 failures (9.1) and the uv pip hint (9.2) are fixed, but the recorded-interpreter mechanism moved the trap into setup. taxi-A-06 rated it major: the agent built a venv, edited README and reran setup through the CLI. On Copilot, each shell step of that recovery needs approval.
consolidated.oct15_ref: fix-plan 9.1, 9.2 (#65); Oct 15 per-run co2-B agent.md item 7 and taxi-B agent.md item 8 (no venv guidance)
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-06: recorded <python-prefix>/bin/python3; awb_mcp.py _python() uses the README line, else .venv/venv, else sys.executable; the setup schema has no interpreter key. co2-A-28: installer error 'README's Project interpreter is <python-prefix>/bin/python3, not this interpreter'. retail-A-17: same fallback, DuckDB missing. taxi-B-34 and retail-B-26: awb-init step 3.3 says 'such as its virtual environment' but never says to create one. co2-B-22: MCP setup conflicts with recording the project venv.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and found none that holds up.

1. The MCP server's interpreter is not a harness invention. kit/setup.sh registers awb with <python-prefix>/bin/python3, through `codex mcp add` in A runs and claude-mcp.json in B runs. That is the 'stable Python 3.10+ outside a project virtual environment' the release README tells users to register (README.md:176-179). `--mcp-config` prints sys.executable, and on this machine that is the same anaconda python3 (3.13.5). Its base install has no duckdb, which I confirmed with an import. Any real user's MCP Python is a global one by design, and duckdb is rarely installed in it.

2. On a fresh project the code records that Python, whatever the host:
- awb_mcp.py:318-319 `_python()` returns project_python(root) or sys.executable.
- awb_cli.py:161-174 checks AWB_PYTHON, then the README line, then .venv/venv, then None.
- The setup command runs install_helpers.py under that interpreter (awb_mcp.py:399-405), and the installer writes its own sys.executable as the Project interpreter (install_helpers.py:196-222).
- The setup inputSchema (awb_mcp.py:191-204) has no interpreter key. Its description never says which interpreter gets recorded.
- After that, a venv interpreter is refused with 'README's Project interpreter is X, not this interpreter' (install_helpers.py:210-212) until README is edited by hand.

3. The skill does not fix the order. awb-init/SKILL.md:32 says to declare packages 'with the interpreter that will run the project's analysis, such as its virtual environment' and to 'Use the awb MCP server's setup tool when the host offers it'. It never says to create a venv before setup, and never says that MCP setup falls back to the server's own Python.

4. The runs reproduce it:
- All 3 Codex-agent runs called MCP setup before any venv existed and recorded <python-prefix>/bin/python3 with in_project false and duckdb missing. The taxi-A agent-001 setup result shows this.
- Each then built a .venv and edited README by hand. co2-A hit the refusal message verbatim (co2-A agent-notes.md:13). retail-A also mis-installed into the user site along the way.
- All 3 Claude-agent runs noted the gap independently. taxi-B and retail-B guessed 'create the venv first' (retail-B notes:8: 'Order (create venv first, then setup) is not stated — I guessed it'). co2-B skipped MCP setup for the CLI because the two instructions conflict (co2-B notes:5).
- Whether an agent avoids the trap depends on its model guessing right, and that is an instruction gap in the release, not a harness artifact.

5. Harness factors I checked:
- Auto-approved MCP tools do not change what setup records.
- The persona front-loading answers and the simulated home are unrelated.
- The PATH order mirrors the real machine. The retail-A referee blamed 'the harness put a base Python 3.13 first on PATH', but that does not apply: the MCP command is an absolute path.
- The Codex sandbox is the one real harness contribution. It would block a global `pip install` into <python-prefix>, which pushed the A agents toward the venv instead of asking the user. On a real host the alternative is asking the user to install duckdb into their base conda. That is still friction caused by the same recording mechanism, and the agents avoided it on judgment anyway.

6. Caveats:
- Four of the evidence IDs the finding cites are wrong. co2-A-28, retail-A-17, taxi-B-34 and retail-B-26 are unrelated findings. The matching ones are co2-A-24, retail-A-21, taxi-B-23 and retail-B-21. co2-B-22 and taxi-A-06 are correct.
- The referees tagged co2-A-24 and retail-A-21 'unclear', citing the environment's interpreter. Point 1 is why I don't accept that.
- 'Major' is arguable. Every run recovered inside the first turn with no user involvement. The Copilot approval cost is inferred from research, not observed.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/awb_mcp.py:318-319 (_python falls back to sys.executable); awb_mcp.py:191-204 (setup schema has no interpreter key; its description does not say which interpreter is recorded); awb_mcp.py:399-405 (setup runs install_helpers.py under _python(root)); awb-init/assets/awb_cli.py:161-174 (project_python order: AWB_PYTHON, README line, .venv/venv, None); awb-init/scripts/install_helpers.py:196-222 (records sys.executable; refuses another interpreter once README names one); awb-init/SKILL.md:32 (says 'such as its virtual environment' and 'Use the awb MCP server's setup tool' with no step to create a venv first); README.md:176-179,196 (register the server with a stable Python outside any venv; the server falls back to its own interpreter)

verdicts.reasoning:
The release causes this. I confirmed it in the shipped code and in the run logs.

Release mechanism:
- The awb/setup inputSchema (awb_mcp.py:191-205) accepts only project, check, upgrade, package_formats, replace and remove_retired. There is no interpreter key.
- write_command('setup') (awb_mcp.py:399-405) runs the installer under _python(root). _python(root) is defined at awb_mcp.py:318-319 as `_cli().project_python(root)[0] or sys.executable`, and project_python (awb_cli.py:161-174) checks AWB_PYTHON, then the README line, then .venv or venv.
- So on a fresh project with no .venv, the installer runs under the MCP server's own interpreter. _interpreter() in install_helpers.py:196-245 then writes that absolute path as `Project interpreter`.
- Once that line is recorded, a run under a new .venv is refused with "README's Project interpreter is X, not this interpreter" (install_helpers.py:209-212). It stays refused until the line is edited by hand, and project_python reads the README line before .venv, so MCP setup keeps picking the recorded interpreter.
- The release's own admin instructions make this the default case. README.md:176 tells admins to register the server with "a stable Python 3.10+ interpreter outside a project virtual environment", which is usually a global Python without duckdb.
- awb-init SKILL.md 3.3 says to install "with the interpreter that will run the project's analysis, such as its virtual environment" and also to "Use the awb MCP server's setup tool". It never says to create a venv first, and never says that setup only picks up a .venv that already exists. The setup tool's description does not say which interpreter it records either.
- The server-resolution order is documented only in the admin section of README.md (line 196) and in the awb_mcp.py docstring, which agents do not see.

Run evidence:
- All three A runs (Codex) called awb/setup on a fresh project, and each recorded `Project interpreter: <python-prefix>/bin/python3` with duckdb missing and in_project false. That Python really lacks duckdb, which I verified. The A runs' setup results are in taxi-A/relay/agent-001.jsonl item_9, co2-A and retail-A turn 1.
- Recovery in the A runs:
  - taxi-A created a .venv, edited the README by script and reran the installer through the CLI.
  - co2-A got the exact refusal string quoted in the finding, then edited the README.
  - retail-A edited the README and reran MCP setup.
- The B runs (Claude Code) guessed the other order. taxi-B and retail-B created the .venv before calling MCP setup, which then recorded .venv/bin/python correctly. co2-B skipped MCP setup and used the CLI, because it could not tell which interpreter setup would record. All three B runs' feedback flags the missing venv guidance. So the "agents guessed the order" claim holds.
- This is not a harness artifact. The harness registered the server with a global python3, exactly as README.md:176 instructs.

Caveats for the synthesizer:
1. The cited IDs are partly wrong. The matching findings are co2-A-24 (co2-A-28 is a relay DEAD-status harness item), retail-A-21 (retail-A-17 is a stock-code finding), taxi-B-23 (taxi-B-34 is a network-premise harness item) and retail-B-21 (retail-B-26 is the upstream ETag probe). taxi-A-06 and co2-B-22 are correct.
2. The severity is arguably overstated. Only taxi-A rated it major; the other five rated it minor or unclear. The refusal message gives a clear remedy, and the README template says "To switch interpreters, edit the line". retail-A shows recovery works through MCP after the README edit, so "had to rerun through the CLI" is not strictly required. Separately, creating the venv and running pip are shell steps on any path, so the extra Copilot approvals come mainly from the redo, not from every step.
3. If the user agrees, installing duckdb into the global interpreter is a designed path (awb-init 3.3 and README Quick-start item 2), so the outcome is not a dead end. Still, nothing in the instructions steers a fresh project toward a project venv, even though the text implies one is preferred.

consolidated.title: Questions reported 'answered' before the user has seen the answers
consolidated.description: The #62 footer now counts the user's own questions, but 'answered' is a ledger status. run.py sets it as soon as a result declares the question, even while the answer still depends on decisions the user has not made. Agents reported '5 answered' and asked for headline approval while chat showed only summaries: leading countries only, rankings promised but not shown, shares without denominators, monthly figures missing. In five runs the user spent a full exchange getting the tables. The headline checkpoint asks for headlines and slide counts, not a summary of the evidence. taxi-B-14 was tagged unclear (a reporting judgment). Product is better evidenced: the footer rule, run.py's marking and the checkpoint format all come from the release, and it recurred in five runs.
consolidated.oct15_ref: new; related to fix-plan 4.1, 4.6 (#62 footer change)
consolidated.evidence: co2-A-03: A2 footer '5 answered with stated caveats'; U3 'I need the actual answers in chat'. retail-A-01: A2 '5 answered · next: headline feedback'; U3. taxi-B-13: run.py marks a question answered when a result declares it; reply 3 '5 answered (provisional)'. taxi-B-14: top-10 and hourly/borough tip tables missing; msg 4. co2-B-09: Q1 figures for 2 of 20 countries; U3. retail-B-12: no 24 monthly figures, unclear unit for '124 cancellations'; U3. Release: AGENTS.md footer; analysis.md 'the run marks those ledger questions answered'; awb-package headline checkpoint.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and did not find one for the core case. The finding's claim that it recurred across five runs is overstated, though.

**The two clear cases, co2-A and retail-A (Codex as the agent):**
- The user answered the scoping questions, asked for preview-and-wait and said "go ahead". The agent then ran landing, analysis and the headline preview in a single turn.
- It ended with "Your five questions: 5 answered" and asked for headline approval. Chat had shown only the headline numbers: the top country for co2 Q1 and Q5, and for retail only one product, 43% overall and no monthly figures. In both runs the user's next message was "I need the actual numbers in chat" before approving.

**Why the harness doesn't explain it:**
- The relay passed every interim agent message, so the user saw everything the agent wrote.
- The Codex agent had no extra system prompt. The harness note asked only for a friction log.
- Sandbox limits, auto-approved MCP tools and the simulated home folder played no part.
- The personas did not invent preview-and-wait or front-loading. The README tells users to put everything in the first message and to say whether they want headlines first, and it says "go ahead" needs no skill name. A real user following the README reaches the same point.
- The persona brief ("do not accept vague answers"; the user must accept all five answers) does push the user to ask for numbers. But a research lead approving donor headlines that name rankings would plausibly ask too, and the README promises "answers come in chat".

**The release supplies each part of the mechanism:**
- The AGENTS.md footer counts ledger status.
- `run.py` marks a question answered as soon as a result declares it.
- In preview-and-wait, the awb-package headline checkpoint shows headlines, the required questions and slide counts, but no summary of the evidence.
- The retail-A agent's own feedback says an evidence summary alongside the headlines would have saved the round.

**Why confidence is medium rather than high:**
1. **The three B runs (Claude as the agent) are a weaker variant.** taxi-B, co2-B and retail-B all gave substantive answers in chat before or alongside the headlines, mostly labelled "provisional". The requests for fuller tables rode along with exchanges already needed for other reasons:
   - taxi-B: two decisions were pending (zero-tip trips and the zone minimum).
   - retail-B: the repeated-lines decision was pending.
   - co2-B: the agent had asked whether to draft the headlines.

   So no extra exchange was spent there, and the referees tagged these minor. "In five runs the user spent a full exchange getting the tables" is not accurate.
2. **The model and the request order matter.** taxi-A used the same Codex agent and release, but the user asked for analysis as its own step. The answers came in chat with full tables in a report, and no exchange was lost. The Claude agents followed AGENTS.md's "Answer in chat"; Codex leaned on the checkpoint format. The release's gap is that it doesn't require the answers to be shown when analysis and the headline preview happen in the same turn.
3. **Some of the cited IDs are wrong.** The actual entries are taxi-B-07 and taxi-B-10, not 13 and 14, and retail-B-09, not 12. The cited taxi-B-13, taxi-B-14 and retail-B-12 describe unrelated issues.

**Conclusion:** this is a real product issue, clearly shown in two runs and in milder form in three. Its severity is closer to costing about one exchange in the front-loaded "go ahead" path than to a major problem in all five runs.
verdicts.release_evidence:
These release files cause it:
- `awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:32`: the turn footer counts the user's questions by ledger status ("Your five questions: 3 answered, 2 open").
- `awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/run.py:16` and `awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md:17`: "When a result declares `answers`, the run marks those ledger questions answered".
- `awb-package/SKILL.md:47` and `awb-package/SKILL.md:52`: preview-and-wait shows the title, the headlines, the required questions and the slide counts, but no summary of the evidence.

These partly contradict it:
- `awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:28` ("Answer in chat, giving file paths") and `README.md:31` ("answers come in chat"). The Claude agents in the B runs followed these and showed the answers. The Codex agents in co2-A and retail-A did not.

verdicts.reasoning:
The release is the cause, and the core claim holds. Some citation details in the finding are wrong; they are listed at the end.

How the release produces "answered" before the user has seen anything:
- AGENTS.md:32 sets the footer to count the user's root questions by their stored ledger status ("Your five questions: 3 answered, 2 open").
- That status is set mechanically. link_answers (awb_provenance.py:2253-2279), which record_finding calls at line 1551, marks a declared question answered as soon as run.py records the result. analysis.md:17 and the run.py docstring (lines 15-16) state the same rule.
- Nothing checks whether the finding is still provisional, whether it depends on a user decision that is still open, or whether the user has seen the figures. The only status the display derives is "awaiting recheck" (awb_provenance.py:2089-2100), and only for flagged or superseded findings. Provisional findings still show as plain answered.

Nothing in the release requires showing the full answer:
- AGENTS.md:28 says "Summarize helper output, quoting it only for a failure or on request". That pushes agents toward summaries rather than the tables the questions ask for.
- The headline checkpoint (awb-package/SKILL.md:47-56) asks for headlines, required questions and slide counts, not the evidence behind each headline.
- The only text pointing the other way is general: "Answer in chat" (AGENTS.md:28) and "answers come in chat" (README:31). Agents did answer in chat, with summaries, so this is not a case of an agent ignoring a clear instruction.

Run evidence (I read the transcripts):
- **co2-A, reply 2 (Codex agent):** the footer reads "5 answered with stated caveats". Chat showed only China's and the US's figures for Q1 and only Greece for Q5. The reply promised "Both top-ten country rankings will appear in full", then asked for headline approval. In U3 the user says "I need the actual answers in chat".
- **retail-A, reply 2 (Codex agent):** the footer reads "5 answered · next: headline feedback". Chat had headlines only: none of Q1's 24 monthly figures, one product for Q4, two countries for Q5. U3 asks for all of them. Codex's own feedback says "the user then needed full tables in chat before approving."
- **taxi-B, reply 3 (Claude agent):** the footer reads "5 answered (provisional), with 2 decisions from you open". Two answers explicitly depended on undecided user choices, and headlines were proposed anyway. In U4 the user asks for the complete weekday/hour, tip-by-hour/borough and top-10 zone tables. The agent's own note (agent.md §1, item 10) blames run.py's marking.
- **co2-B, reply 2 (Claude agent):** the footer reads "all answered". All 20 Q1 countries were named, but only 3 had figures (the finding says 2). The Q2 list had no numbers. U3 asks for them.
- **retail-B, reply 2 (Claude agent):** the footer reads "all answered (provisional)". There were no 24 monthly figures and no cohort counts, and the unit of "124 cancellations" was unclear. U3 asks for them.

The pattern appears with both the Codex and Claude agents, so it is not one model's habit. Each case cost the user one exchange. On a normal interactive host a real user would see the same footer and the same checkpoint. The persona's "Do not accept vague answers" rule in BRIEF.md made the simulated users strict, but a real user who asked "which 10 countries" would also ask to see the ten.

Corrections the finding needs:
- **Wrong IDs:** the IDs taxi-B-13, taxi-B-14 and retail-B-12 point to unrelated items. The matching entries in findings.json are taxi-B-07, taxi-B-10 and retail-B-09.
- **Wrong tag:** taxi-B-10 is tagged product, not unclear.
- **Wrong count:** co2-B-09 says 3 of 20, not 2 of 20.
- **Overstated scope:** only co2-A, retail-A and taxi-B asked for headline approval in the same reply. co2-B and retail-B reported "answered" and offered headlines as the next step.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:32 (footer counts root questions by ledger status); awb-init/assets/awb_provenance.py:2253-2279 with call at :1551 (link_answers marks a declared question answered when run.py records even a provisional result); awb-init/assets/awb_provenance.py:2089-2100 (only flagged/superseded findings change the displayed status); awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md:17 and investigation/run.py:15-16 (run marks ledger questions answered); awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:28 ("Summarize helper output, quoting it only for a failure or on request"); awb-package/SKILL.md:47-56 (headline checkpoint shows headlines, required questions and slide counts, not the evidence)

consolidated.title: Agents run awb helpers through the terminal instead of the registered MCP tools
consolidated.description: With the awb MCP server connected, the Opus agents ran land, publish, sql, export, check-draft, state, questions, review-rules, release and run.py as Bash CLI calls in every turn. They used MCP only for a few read and records calls, although AGENTS.md says to use the MCP tools whenever the host offers them. Every SKILL.md, the review brief and workbench-guides/analysis.md spell commands as 'python3 src/awb.py ...' or 'python3 investigations/<name>/run.py', which pulls toward the CLI. On Copilot, which cannot auto-approve terminal calls, or on Claude Code in default mode, each call would need approval. The harness pre-allowed Bash (C-67), which hid that cost. Oct 15 could not show this, because its Opus agents had no MCP server.
consolidated.oct15_ref: new (Oct 15 Opus agents had no MCP server); related to fix-plan 9.5b (#65)
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-06: Bash helper calls per turn 1/15/17/8/34/14/6 vs mcp__awb calls 2/1/4/2/1/0/0; the agent cites 'habit'. co2-B-32: about 32 MCP calls vs hundreds of Bash calls (A5 214, A7 221, including subagents). retail-B-09: MCP used only for setup, read status/stale, clean-record, clean-scan and release. taxi-A-36: analysis.md line 17 runs run.py directly, while AGENTS.md routes it through awb/run. Release: AGENTS.md Commands routing rule; awb-package step 4 'Run python3 src/awb.py export...'.

verdicts.reasoning:
I couldn't find a harness cause for the behaviour itself. The one harness effect is that it hid what the behaviour would cost a real user.

What the harness did and did not change:
- **Pre-allowing Bash.** relay.py passes `--allowedTools Bash,...,mcp__awb` with an auto-approving `--permission-prompt-tool`, and the logs record almost no prompts. That hides the approval cost, as C-67 says. It can't explain the choice of tool: the model doesn't see which tools are pre-allowed, and in interactive default mode MCP calls prompt too.
- **MCP was connected and working.** The awb server shows as connected in every Opus init event, and all seven awb tools are listed. Across the three Opus runs, 42 MCP calls produced exactly one error, a genuine RecordError from the agent's own input. No harness failure pushed the agents to the CLI.
- **The simulation prompt points toward MCP, not away.** claude-agent-system.md says outright that the awb MCP server is registered.
- **MCP tools were deferred behind ToolSearch.** taxi-B loaded only setup/read/records/data, so run, package and release stayed unloaded. This is how real Claude Code behaves, not something the harness added.
- **The agents' own reasons apply to any host.** All three Opus agents give the same two reasons: habit, and being able to pipe CLI output through filters. In taxi-B, 63 of 88 helper calls in turns 2-7 were piped or chained.

Recount of main-thread helper calls, Bash vs MCP:

| Run | Bash helper calls | MCP calls | Reviewer subagents (Bash) |
|---|---|---|---|
| taxi-B | 87 | 10 | 21 |
| co2-B | 93 | 32 | 38 |
| retail-B | 69 | 10 | 15 |

Why the release is a cause:
- The Opus agents used MCP almost only where AGENTS.md:20 names a specific MCP route for a skill script: clean-scan, clean-record, eda-scan, status, setup.
- Everything spelled as `python3 src/awb.py ...` went through Bash: land, publish, sql, state, questions, export, check-draft, release, review-rules, and run.py.
- AGENTS.md:24, four lines after the routing rule, says "Run workbench helpers with `python3 src/awb.py <command>`".
- analysis.md:17 runs run.py directly.
- review.md:10 and :18 tell Claude Code reviewer subagents to use Bash and the CLI. So the subagent CLI calls are by design, not deviations.
- Installed copies of AGENTS.md and analysis.md match the release byte for byte.

A real Opus user on interactive Claude Code would get the same choices. Model behaviour also plays a part, though: the Codex agents on the same release mostly used MCP. taxi-A had about 126 MCP calls against roughly 11 CLI helper calls, mostly install_helpers runs and inline Python edits.

Corrections to the finding:
1. taxi-A does not show the behaviour. It supports only the wording inconsistency in analysis.md:17.
2. co2-B's "214/221" counts all Bash calls, file reads and edits included, not helper calls. The helper-only count is 93 CLI to 32 MCP. co2-B turn 2 also made 16 MCP records calls, so "only a few read and records calls" overstates the case.
3. On Claude Code default mode, MCP calls prompt too. The cost gap there comes from how approvals can be remembered: you can always-allow a whole MCP tool, but Bash approvals go by command prefix, and the agents' chained heredoc commands defeat those. The Copilot cost is extrapolated: no Copilot run was made, so whether Opus on Copilot would prefer the terminal is unshown.

Severity "major" stands for Copilot users, if Copilot behaves as assumed, and is smaller on Claude Code.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:20 (MCP routing rule) contradicted by AGENTS.md:24 ("Run workbench helpers with `python3 src/awb.py <command>`"); workbench-guides/analysis.md:17 ("Run `python3 investigations/<name>/run.py`"); awb-package/SKILL.md:37,45,68,78 and awb-release/SKILL.md:22,24 spell the CLI; awb-status/SKILL.md:42-49 actions table spells the CLI; awb-package/references/review.md:10,18 tell Claude Code reviewer subagents to use Bash and `python3 src/awb.py review-rules check`. Harness side: kit/relay.py `--allowedTools Bash,...,mcp__awb` plus the auto-approve prompt tool hides the prompt cost but doesn't cause the behaviour.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core claim holds up, and the release is a real cause. Some of the cited evidence is overstated.

What the runs show (I counted tool calls in relay/agent-*.jsonl myself):
- In every B run, the init event lists the `awb` server as connected, with all 7 `mcp__awb__*` tools.
- taxi-B, Bash calls to awb helpers per turn: 1/15/17/8/47/14/10 (subagents included). MCP calls per turn: 2/1/4/2/1/0/0. That matches the finding.
- co2-B: 32 MCP calls in total, all `records` state/questions and `read` help/status. Over Bash: `check-draft` 49, `review-rules check` 38, `sql` 18, `export` 10, `run.py` 6, plus `land`, `publish` and `release`.
- retail-B: MCP was used only for `setup`, `clean-scan`, `clean-record`, `read` status/stale and `release`. `run.py`, `export`, `check-draft`, `state`, `questions` and `sql` all went through the CLI.
- All three Opus agents say in feedback/agent.md that they chose the CLI 'out of habit' and to pipe JSON through filters. retail-B's agent admits AGENTS.md prefers MCP.
- The pattern is telling. The agents used MCP for exactly the skill scripts that AGENTS.md maps one by one (`scan_dataset.py` to `clean-scan`, `record_cleaning.py` to `clean-record`, `eda_scan.py`, `collect_status.py`, `install_helpers.py`). They fell back to the CLI for everything the skills and guides spell as `python3 src/awb.py ...` or `run.py`. So AGENTS.md was in context: the project has no CLAUDE.md, and the runs used Claude Code 2.1.301. The general rule lost out to the literal command spellings.

Why the release is a cause:
- The MCP preference is one sentence: AGENTS.md line 20.
- AGENTS.md itself then says, with no condition, 'Run workbench helpers with `python3 src/awb.py <command>`' (line 24). Line 7 and the Record maintenance section use the same CLI wording.
- About 85 CLI spellings sit across the SKILL.md files, the guides and the references. Among the SKILL.md files, only awb-init mentions MCP.
- workbench-guides/analysis.md line 17 says, with no condition, 'Run `python3 investigations/<name>/run.py`'. taxi-A's agent flagged this as contradicting AGENTS.md.
- awb-package/references/review.md tells Claude Code reviewers to run `python3 src/awb.py review-rules check` with Bash; only Copilot gets the MCP call. Those reviewer calls follow the release's instructions rather than ignoring them.
- README line 198 confirms this is deliberate: the skills keep their CLI commands and rely on the AGENTS.md rule alone. Three of three Opus runs ignored that rule many times.

Harness role:
- relay.py passes `--allowedTools Bash,...` and auto-approves every prompt (`--permission-prompt-tool mcp__simperm__approve`), so in co2-B the run hit only 1 permission prompt.
- That hid the approval cost, but it did not cause the tool choice. The model is not told which tools are pre-allowed. A real Claude Code user in default mode would see Bash approval prompts. On Copilot, the target host, terminal calls cannot be auto-approved.

Where the finding overstates:
- taxi-A had a Codex agent, not Opus, and it followed the routing rule well (for example turn 2: 17 read, 22 records, 7 data, 2 run). The same goes for co2-A and retail-A. taxi-A only supports the analysis.md inconsistency, so the problem shows up for Claude on Claude Code, not for every agent.
- co2-B's 214 and 221 are all Bash calls in those turns, including cat and sed. Helper Bash calls there were 32 and 26.
- The reviewer `review-rules check` calls over Bash follow review.md, so they are not deviations from it.

These caveats make the finding narrower and lower my confidence to medium. They do not overturn it.

consolidated.title: Review rules recorded on the agent's judgment: unasked, overbroad or draft-specific, with no precedence
consolidated.description: review.md tells the agent to turn a correction into a numbered rule before repairing, with no step asking the user whether the correction is general. Agents saved rules without asking (four in taxi-A, four in co2-A). Some rules hard-code one draft's figures into the project-wide foundation/review-rules.md. One rule was broader than the user's correction and conflicted with another rule, and the release gives no precedence guidance. In co2-B, the agent-written R-periods-001 was applied to the title and Answer slides, which bloated the subtitle and the Answer caveat. The same co2-B R-periods-001 over-literal rule was Oct 15's 6.2 example, and #66's Scope field did not prevent it.
consolidated.oct15_ref: fix-plan 6.2 (#66 rule Scope field); Oct 15 per-run co2-B agent.md item 4 (same R-periods-001 rule)
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-09: R-tipping-001, R-fare-definitions-001, R-question-coverage-001 and R-zone-display-001 saved without asking. co2-A-10: four rules saved without asking. co2-A-11: R-consumption-001 hard-codes 'US and EU-27 figures rise and China's and India's figures fall'. taxi-B-11: R-rates-001 and R-methodology-note-001 conflict on one line, and the note reached 541 words. co2-B-06: the subtitle listed every period ('the reviewer asked for every period to be named'); U7 restored it. Release: review.md 'After the review'; awb-package SKILL.md line 22; README lines 103 and 135.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to pin this on the harness and could not.

1. Possible harness causes, and why each fails:
- The relay blocks AskUserQuestion for the Claude agent (kit/relay.py:36-38), and Codex exec has no mid-turn ask either. That does not explain the result. The release never tells the agent to ask in the first place. review.md:39 says the agent should "decide whether later drafts could repeat the mistake. If they could, record the correction as a rule before repairing", then report the new ID. Agents could still end a turn with a question, and they did when the release required one, for example at the preview-and-wait headline checkpoints in taxi-A and co2-A.
- The behavior is the same in all six runs, under both models. Codex agents (taxi-A, co2-A) and Claude agents (taxi-B, co2-B, retail-B) all saved rules without asking. retail-A saved 8 rules and retail-B 6. This is the release's instruction being followed, not one model's quirk.
- The user corrections were realistic bundled review notes, not a persona front-loading answers.
- The README tells the user rules are recorded automatically (README:103, 135), and awb-package SKILL.md:22 repeats the agent-decides rule. Nothing in the harness changes this path.

2. Each claim checked against the run folders:
- **Unasked rules.** taxi-A saved R-tipping-001, R-fare-definitions-001, R-question-coverage-001 and R-zone-display-001, reported only after the fact in replies 6 and 7. co2-A saved R-headlines-001, R-headlines-002, R-consumption-001 and R-metric-definitions-001, also unasked.
- **Draft-specific rules in the project-wide file.** Three taxi-A rules begin "For this board study". co2-A R-consumption-001 requires stating that "the US and EU-27 figures rise and China's and India's figures fall". Both sit in foundation/review-rules.md, although the release says a one-off correction is an edit, not a rule.
- **Broad rule and conflict.** In taxi-B the user's Newark-only request became the general R-rates-001. At release review it forced a line into the methods note, which reached 541 words against R-methodology-note-001. The release gives no precedence guidance; grep finds none. The only implicit way out is error versus warning severity, and the agent trimmed the note instead.
- **co2-B.** The agent's own notes say its R-periods-001, worded more strictly than the user's "keep relevant years and caveats", was "applied strictly to the Answer slide too, forcing a very long combined Caveat bullet". The reviewer flagged R-periods-001 violations at findings.md:5 (the Answer slide) in several rounds. The Oct 15 run had the same over-literal reading (docs/ux-simulation-2026-10-15/fix-plan.md 6.2). The rule now carries Scope: slide and the problem recurred.

3. Corrections to the finding:
- Several evidence IDs are mis-cited. co2-A-10 is about the deliverable boundary and co2-A-11 about START-HERE; the rules finding is co2-A-09. taxi-B-11 is about airport fees; the conflict finding is taxi-B-22.
- The co2-B subtitle bloat was raised as a narrative problem, not as an R-periods-001 violation. It traces partly to the writer's own addition to the reviewer brief ("check that each headline's and subtitle's periods attach to the right claims") and to the user's earlier subtitle request. So the title-slide part of the claim is only partly the rule's doing. The Answer-slide caveat bloat is directly the rule's.
- The per-run findings were tagged minor except co2-B-06, so "major" may overstate it.

None of this points to the harness. The core mechanism is in the release: the agent decides and words rules alone, with no confirmation step, no guard against draft-specific rules, and no precedence when rules conflict.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/references/review.md:39 (the agent decides whether a correction becomes a rule and records it before repairing; no step asks the user; the only ask in 'After the review', line 35, is for a broken rule's unclear intent); awb-package/SKILL.md:22 (record the correction as a rule first when later drafts could repeat it); README.md:103 and README.md:135 (rules recorded automatically from corrections); no precedence or conflict guidance anywhere in awb-package/, awb-release/ or README.md (grep), only error/warning severity (awb_draft.py review-rules add help)

verdicts.reasoning:
The core of the finding holds, and the release causes it. Some of the supporting claims are wrong or weak, though.

**Release text**
- review.md:39 hands the decision to the agent alone: "decide whether later drafts could repeat the mistake. If they could, record the correction as a rule before repairing." It then says to report the new ID, and nothing asks the user first.
- awb-package SKILL.md:22, README.md:135 ("is appended there as a numbered rule") and the project AGENTS.md:50 all describe the same automatic append.
- The only place a rule can go is the project-wide foundation/review-rules.md, which is checked on every draft. There is no rule scoped to one package or investigation.
- The "later drafts could repeat it" test also covers later revisions of the same package. A correction that only concerns one deck therefore passes the test. The only counter-example the release gives is narrow: "a preferred wording on one slide".
- The Scope field (CHANGELOG line 35, awb_draft.py `_SCOPES`) only sets how much text one violation covers. It does not limit which slides a rule applies to.
- No release text says which rule wins when two conflict.

**Run evidence that confirms the finding**
- taxi-A, replies 6 and 7: the agent saved R-tipping-001, R-fare-definitions-001, R-question-coverage-001 and R-zone-display-001 without asking. Three of them open with "For this board study", and R-tipping-001 fixes this deck's framing ("about a quarter of fare in both months") in the project-wide file.
- co2-A, replies 3 to 5: the agent saved four rules without asking. Reply 4 never mentions R-headlines-002 or R-consumption-001, and R-consumption-001 hard-codes "the US and EU-27 figures rise and China's and India's figures fall".
- The simulated users in both runs complained (taxi-A human.md pain point 3; co2-A human.md pain point 3).
- taxi-B and co2-B (Claude agents) also saved rules without asking, but their rules are general.

**Problems with the finding as written**
1. Three evidence IDs are wrong. co2-A-10, co2-A-11 and taxi-B-11 are about other issues (the deliverable boundary, START-HERE wording, and airport-fee analysis). The matching findings are co2-A-09 and taxi-B-22.
2. The taxi-B conflict is real but small. R-rates-001 is an error-level rule and R-methodology-note-001 a warning, and the release's severity model already lets the user accept a warning. The agent trimmed the note back to about 500 words and the final review was clean. The 541 words was a passing state. "No precedence guidance" is literally true.
3. The co2-B subtitle growth was not caused by R-periods-001. In agent-006.jsonl line 179 the reviewer reports "R-periods-001 pass" and flags the subtitle as a step-3 narrative problem instead. The writing agent had added "check that each headline's and subtitle's periods attach to the right claims" to the reviewer's brief.
4. The co2-B Answer-caveat growth did come from R-periods-001 (violations at findings.md:5 "## Answer"). But the writing agent's own brief told the reviewer that the Answer slide carries a combined Caveat bullet. The rule also closely follows the user's message 4 ("Keep relevant years and caveats on the slides they qualify"). The agent's added phrase "as a Caveat bullet" is what made the rule overly literal.
5. "Major" severity looks overstated. The per-run findings were rated minor (taxi-A-09, co2-A-09, taxi-B-22), and the one major item, co2-B-06, is partly blamed on the wrong cause.

**Verdict:** product. The part to keep is that review.md gives the agent unilateral authority to write rules into a project-wide file that has no package scope. The conflict and co2-B claims should be weakened or dropped.

No precedence text anywhere in review.md. Contradicting evidence for the co2-B subtitle part: co2-B/relay/agent-006.jsonl line 179 reports "R-periods-001 pass" and flags the subtitle as a narrative problem.

consolidated.title: Standard reconciliation checks are not set up with results, so 'checked' claims surface late and force reruns
consolidated.description: Validation leaves row_counts and joins 'not assessed' unless a producer supplies counts, and analysis.md's 'Add a result' suggests no standard reconciliation or coverage checks. Meanwhile #66's review brief requires every 'checked', 'reconciles' or 'matches' sentence to cite a recorded check. The gap surfaces only at packaging. Every finding carried a 'not assessed' caveat, and taxi-B's methods text told the board that counts and joins were not checked. Users expected totals to have been reconciled already. Adding the checks meant new run.py results linked to questions they do not answer, producer changes, reruns, re-export and re-promotion. The evidence format records only the last step's counts, which is too thin for the tolerance claims (C-10). review.md does not say how foundation scans or external checks satisfy the citation rule. The boilerplate 'joins not assessed' caveat was already present in Oct 15 taxi-B and co2-B; the late cost is new with #66.
consolidated.oct15_ref: Oct 15 per-run taxi-B agent.md item 5 and co2-B agent-notes (joins always not assessed); side effect of fix-plan 6.3 (#66 change 4, #63 change 5)
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-03: the settings.toml template records an omitted key as 'not assessed'; state.md rows still read 'not assessed: row_counts, joins'. retail-B-06: A6 commits 6fb0cc2, c18e2e7 and c1e1393 added the checks; the user 'expected basic totals to have been reconciled already'. co2-B-16: hard-coded before=216 / after=20 to avoid 'not assessed'. co2-B-39: world-reconciliation and q4-missing-years registered under Q-004. taxi-A-34: the first full review failed on two missing citations (duplicate scan, OPM dates). retail-B-35: awb_validate.py line 120 records only 'Steps checked: N; last X -> Y rows'.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and did not find one. The mechanism lives in the release, and it showed up in runs where the user never pressed for it.

1) The defaults are in the release code. run.py's default producer returns `{}`. validate() records any absent spec key as not assessed. The settings template says runtime counts are "Usually from a producer". analysis.md:17 lets the agent close a not_assessed entry with a caveat instead of a check. In taxi-B, 17 of 19 state.md rows carry "not assessed: row_counts, joins". That includes record-reconciliation, the result that performs the check.

2) The late cost comes from #66's citation rule. review.md:22 and package-contract.md:48 accept only a result ID or evidence path in methodology.md. In co2-B the agent had already reconciled countries against World during cleaning, recorded as exploration/country-world-reconciliation.sql and DQ-004. At packaging, turn 4, the reviewer refused that citation: it "cites only an exploration query", and the declared duplicate/key checks "no evidence file records". The agent then built world-reconciliation and q4-missing-years as run.py results. Because a result needs a question, it reused Q-004's question text (settings.toml), invented a 0.15 Mt tolerance, and reran and re-exported. This happened with no user prompting, so neither the persona nor the relay caused it. In taxi-A, Codex's first full review failed on missing duplicate-scan and OPM-date citations. That agent then asked for review.md to say how foundation scans and external checks count. Nothing in review.md answers that.

3) The user-triggered cases are plausible user behaviour, not persona front-loading. Neither the taxi-B brief nor human-rules.md mentions reconciliation. Dana asked only after the methods note told the board that row counts and joins weren't checked. The retail-B user asked for plain-language "totals reconcile" wording, and the agent correctly saw that the citation rule needed new recorded results (commit 6fb0cc2, then two more).

4) Nothing in the harness touches this. Non-interactive mode, auto-approved MCP, the sandbox and the simulated home all leave validation defaults and review rules alone. The agent system prompt says only "behave exactly as you normally would." The agent models are the ones real users run.

5) awb_validate.py:120 does record only the step count and the last step's before/after counts.

Caveats that narrow the finding without overturning it:
- "Every finding carried a 'not assessed' caveat" is true only of taxi-B. taxi-A, co2-B and retail-B supplied row_counts and joins, co2-B through hard-coded before=216 / after=20 numbers.
- analysis.md:13 does tell the agent to specify counts before and after each filter and join checks. The taxi-B agent partly departed from that. What analysis.md lacks is a standard reconciliation (input = kept + excluded) and coverage checks, which the finding correctly says.
- Several cited evidence IDs (retail-B-06, retail-B-35, co2-B-39, taxi-A-34) do not match the IDs in findings.json. I checked the substance directly instead.
- I could not check the Oct 15 comparison against those runs.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/run.py:53-54 (default producer returns {}, nothing measured); awb-init/assets/awb_validate.py:182-183 (absent key recorded as not-applicable/'not assessed') and :120 (only 'Steps checked: N; last X -> Y rows'); awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/settings.toml:14 (question required), :32 ('Usually from a producer'), :35 (omitted key recorded as not assessed); awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md:13 (asks for counts and joins, but no reconciliation or coverage result) and :17 (not_assessed may be closed with a caveat); awb-package/references/review.md:22 and awb-package/references/package-contract.md:48 (every checked/reconciles/matches sentence must cite a result ID or evidence path; foundation scans and external checks not mentioned). Run evidence: co2-B/relay/agent-004.jsonl rows 174-192 (reviewer rejects the exploration-query and DQ-004 citations; the agent then builds world-reconciliation); co2-B/project/investigations/co2-cuts-growth-consumption/settings.toml:128-142 (both results reuse Q-004's question); taxi-B state.md (17 of 19 rows not assessed); taxi-B/transcript.md:458 (user asks for reconciliation); retail-B/transcript.md:427-473 and human/feedback.md:13.

verdicts.reasoning:
The shipped files cause this, and the run evidence shows it. Four parts of the release combine.

(1) Validation defaults. In awb_validate.validate(), a spec key that is absent is recorded as "not-applicable / not assessed". run.py's default producer "measures nothing". The settings.toml template's example validation omits row_counts and joins and says runtime counts come "usually from a producer". Meanwhile analysis.md:11 says only a result that needs more than its query gets a producer. That leaves a query-only result two options: a 'not assessed' caveat, or hard-coded static counts. co2-B did the second (before=216, after=20 in settings.toml:24), which makes the check vacuous. analysis.md:17 explicitly lets an unassessed check be "justified with a caveat".

(2) No reconciliation or coverage check is suggested anywhere on the analysis side. analysis.md:13 lists columns, per-filter counts, joins and nulls only.

(3) The package templates ask for exactly that kind of claim. findings-template.md:66 and methodology-note-template.md:29 both prompt for "totals reconcile to the finance ledger within 0.5%".

(4) The new review rule (review.md:22 and package-contract.md:48, listed as new under Unreleased at CHANGELOG.md:36) turns any such sentence without a cited "result ID or evidence path" into a narrative problem. It does not say whether a foundation quality record, an exploration query or an external check counts.

So the gap only shows up at packaging, even for an agent that follows the analysis guide fully. retail-B and co2-B had no 'not assessed' rows at all, and both still had to add reconciliation checks late.

What the run evidence shows:
- taxi-B: 17 of 18 state.md rows read "not assessed: row_counts, joins". In user message 6 (relay/agent-006.in.md) the user says "The methods text says row counts and joins weren't checked" and asks for a reconciliation. The agent then added record-reconciliation, reran, re-exported and re-promoted. Even that reconciliation result carries the not-assessed caveat (history.md:190).
- co2-B: the reconciliation was done early, as an exploration query and DQ-004. The reviewer rejected it: "cites only an exploration query. It gives no result ID or evidence path" (relay/agent-004.jsonl line 174). That forced a new world-reconciliation run.py result at packaging (line 189), filed under Q-004's question text, and later q4-missing-years. agent.md section 4 admits neither answers Q-004.
- retail-B: commit c18e2e7 changed a producer and regenerated evidence after the findings were accepted. human.md item 3 has the quote "I expected basic totals to have been reconciled already".
- taxi-A: agent-notes.md:87 records that the first full review failed on two missing completed-check citations (duplicate scan, OPM dates).
- awb_validate.py:120 records only the last step's counts.

Caveats on the finding as written:
- "Every finding carried a 'not assessed' caveat" is true of taxi-B only. The other five runs show 0 such rows.
- Several evidence labels do not match findings.json. retail-B-06 there is about cross-sheet duplicates; retail-B-35 is a harness item about the persona; co2-B-39 and taxi-A-34 do not exist (co2-B has 31 items, taxi-A has 29). I checked the cited facts directly in the relays, commits, feedback files and code instead.
- taxi-B's agent did skip analysis.md:13's per-filter counts. But the release allows that with a caveat, and complying would not have produced the totals reconciliation the package templates ask for.

Nothing here depends on the harness. A real interactive user would hit the same review gate.
