consolidated.title: No supported way to share code or SQL across results within an investigation
consolidated.description: run.py loads producers with spec_from_file_location and puts only ROOT on sys.path, so a producer cannot import a sibling module. Agents added sys.path.insert to every producer, and the analysis guide does not say how to import a shared module. There is no view or shared SQL local to the investigation, so taxi-B copied a ~20-line screening CTE into more than 15 files and repeated the rules as literals in [eda]. taxi-A also found that parallel DuckDB aggregation changed floating-point tails between runs until threads=1 was set.
consolidated.oct15_ref: new; related to fix-plan 5.1 (#63 per-result producer modules)
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-21. retail-B-23: run.py lines 37 and 82; agent-002 call 36. taxi-B-25: queries/*.sql and settings.toml [eda].

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and found none. Every part of the finding comes from release code or docs that the projects copied unchanged: diff shows retail-B's and taxi-B's run.py are byte-identical to the release template, and taxi-A's produced no diff either. None of it depends on non-interactive runs, the Codex sandbox, auto-approved MCP, the simulated home folder, relay or personas.

1. Imports. The MCP run tool and the CLI both start run.py as `python <abs>/run.py` with the environment unchanged, so the run behaves the same as a normal host. run.py loads producers with spec_from_file_location and adds only ROOT to sys.path. A helper in producers/ therefore cannot be imported with a plain import. retail-B worked this out in advance (agent-002 call 36 wrote `from line_counts import line_counts`; call 37 added sys.path.insert to five producers before any run).

2. Shared SQL. The release gives no place for investigation-local SQL. session() loads only foundation/views. awb-clean sends user-chosen exclusions to "that investigation's settings", where the only tool is $parameters. The [eda] where list in eda_scan.py reads [parameters] only for start and end. So taxi-B's 20-line screening CTE (parameterised) sits in all 17 queries/*.sql files, and the same rules appear as literals in [eda].

3. Floating-point tails. A rerun is matched to the prior run by the sha256 of the result CSV. DuckDB's parallel float sums vary in the last digits, and the release neither pins threads nor allows a tolerance. Any rerun can therefore demote a supported finding. taxi-A had to put `SET threads=1` in its producer.

The finding overstates some points:
- Code can be shared. The guide and run.py docstring say "put reusable operations in src/", and src/ is importable. A helper.py in the investigation folder itself also imports, because running run.py as a script puts its folder on sys.path (I confirmed this with a test script). The settings template's example `code = ["helpers.py"]` even assumes such a helper. The real gap is that the guide names "a helper module in the investigation folder" but never says how to import one.
- "Agents added sys.path.insert to every producer" is true only of retail-B. taxi-A used `import_module("investigations.taxi-trip-patterns.producers.analysis_common")` through ROOT, and taxi-B had no producers.
- The cited finding IDs are wrong. taxi-A-21, retail-B-23 and taxi-B-25 are unrelated awb-status/awb-clean items. The matching entries are taxi-A-19, retail-B-18 and taxi-B-13.

Even narrowed to these points (no investigation-local views or shared SQL, an undocumented import pattern, and exact-hash reruns without pinned threads), a real user on an interactive host would hit this, and the release is the cause. Minor severity fits.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/run.py:37 (sys.path.insert(0, ROOT) only) and :82-88 (spec_from_file_location/exec_module, producer folder never added to the path); run.py:18 and workbench-guides/analysis.md:7 ("put reusable operations in src/", which contradicts "no supported way" for code); analysis.md:11 (mentions "a helper module in the investigation folder" but gives no import pattern); awb_landing.py:1156-1159 (session loads only foundation/views, so no investigation-local views); awb-clean/SKILL.md:28 (investigation-local exclusions go to settings); awb-explore/scripts/eda_scan.py:109-127 ([eda] where does not expand [parameters]); awb_provenance.py:1435-1437 and :1515-1521 (exact-match rerun compares the table's sha256, and nothing pins threads or sets a float tolerance)

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding is half right. The shared-SQL part is real and the release causes it. The Python-import part is mostly wrong, and the floating-point part is a separate issue folded in.

SQL duplication (real, caused by the release):
- run.py opens `session(ROOT)`, which loads only `foundation/views` (awb_landing.py:1156-1157). Nothing in the release gives an investigation its own views.
- The data guide says filters and exclusions are local to the investigation (data.md:43), and awb-clean says investigation-local exclusions go in settings. But settings can hold only scalar `[parameters]`.
- awb-explore SKILL.md:41 tells the agent to "copy every printed scope filter, period included, into its WHERE" for every exploration query.
- `[eda] where` is raw SQL with no `$parameter` substitution (eda_scan.py:108-131, 632-634).
- I confirmed in taxi-B: the screening CTE appears in 17 files under queries/ and exploration/, and `settings.toml [eda] where` repeats the same rules as literal numbers (6*3600, 100, 500, 60).
- A workaround does exist, though it is undocumented as a sharing pattern: list a shared SQL file in each result's `queries` and run it from a producer. taxi-A did exactly this (`queries = [..., "queries/analysis-records.sql", ...]`, with the producer creating a temp table from sql[1]). It costs a producer for every result. So "no supported way" overstates the gap, but a real user would still meet it.

Python import (mostly unsupported):
- The claim that run.py "puts only ROOT on sys.path, so a producer cannot import a sibling module" is inaccurate. The MCP tool runs `[python, run.py]` as a normal script (awb_mcp.py:398), so Python also puts the investigation folder on sys.path.
- I tested this in a scratch copy of run.py's loader:
  - `from helpers import X`, with helpers.py in the investigation folder, works.
  - `from producers.common import X` works.
  - Only a bare `from common import X`, for a module inside producers/, fails.
- The analysis guide's own example (`code = ["helpers.py"]`, "a helper module in the investigation folder") is therefore importable. src/, which the release names as the home for reusable code (analysis.md:7, run.py:18), is on sys.path too. The gap is one missing sentence about the import form.
- "Agents added sys.path.insert to every producer" is true only of retail-B. That agent put its helper in producers/ rather than the investigation folder. It added the inserts at call 37, before its first run.py run at call 38, so it was preventing a failure it expected; none had occurred. taxi-A used `import_module("investigations.taxi-trip-patterns.producers.analysis_common")`, which works without any sys.path edit.

Floating-point tails (real, but a separate issue):
- A rerun keeps a finding's row only if the saved table's sha256 is unchanged (awb_provenance.py:1436-1454; analysis.md "unchanged table"). The release never sets DuckDB threads or mentions float rounding or tolerance.
- So taxi-A's run-to-run changes in sums and means (agent-notes.md:49) do come from the release. They should be filed as their own finding, not under code sharing.

Cited IDs:
- taxi-A-21, retail-B-23 and taxi-B-25 in each run's findings.json are about awb-status and awb-clean, not this issue, so the citation IDs do not match.
- The underlying evidence does exist elsewhere: taxi-A agent.md row 14; retail-B agent.md item 8 and agent-notes.md:25; taxi-B agent.md item 4; plus the project files.

Recommendation: narrow C-41 to "no documented investigation-local shared SQL or view; awb-explore instructs copying filters; [eda] where cannot read [parameters]". Fold the import point into a one-line doc note, and split the determinism issue out.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/run.py:163 (`session(ROOT)` loads only foundation/views; awb-init/assets/awb_landing.py:1156-1157 defaults views_dir to "foundation/views"); awb-explore/SKILL.md:41 ("copy every printed scope filter ... into its WHERE"); awb-explore/scripts/eda_scan.py:108-131,632-634 (`[eda] where` is raw SQL, no parameter substitution). Contradicting the import claim: run.py:18 and analysis.md:7 put reusable code in src/ (run.py:37 puts ROOT on sys.path); analysis.md:11 names "a helper module in the investigation folder", which imports because awb_mcp.py:398 runs run.py as a script, so the investigation folder is also on sys.path. Floating-point part: awb_provenance.py:1436-1454 compares the table by exact sha256; no threads or tolerance guidance anywhere in the release.

consolidated.title: Quality-ledger writer cannot amend observations, and it bloats or pads entries
consolidated.description: record_cleaning keeps an entry's original observation, so a withdrawn claim (DQ-008's World-series observation) stays, and a wrong Libya observation needed a hand edit. clean-record requires a 'findings' string even when no view changed. Recording a clean scan created separate rows for the raw and canonical forms of the same issues (DQ-007 to DQ-025).
consolidated.evidence: co2-B-15: record_cleaning.py:20 and :328. taxi-B-41: clean-record call with only a DQ-013 revision. taxi-A-20: project/foundation/quality.md.

verdicts.reasoning:
I found no harness cause for the main claim. Two of the three sub-claims are overstated or come from agent choices.

1) Cannot amend an observation (co2-B). This is real, and the release causes it on purpose. The record_cleaning.py docstring (line 20) says a quality-ID key "revises only judgment cells, keeps the observation and link." awb-clean/SKILL.md:69 says "the observation stays as first written." A `new` entry is matched by object plus observation (record_cleaning.py:410-425), so resubmitting it with corrected text adds a second row instead of fixing the first. In co2-B, message 7, the persona asked for a legitimate correction: matching totals do not show how OWID built the World series. The agent (Claude) told the user "The project's data-quality log can't rewrite an entry's original description." DQ-008 in co2-B/project/foundation/quality.md still contains "so World omits them too", with the withdrawal added to the treatment cell only. Earlier the agent fixed its own Libya error (DQ-007) by hand-editing the file, so a hand edit works but no helper supports it. No harness factor explains any of this: not the non-interactive relay, the sandbox, auto-approved MCP, or front-loading by the persona. A real user who needed to correct an observation would hit it. The cited line :328 ("the original observation wins") is about scan baselines versus rescans, not amendment, so that citation is slightly off.

2) "findings required even when no view changed" (taxi-B) is overstated. The script requires findings only when a decision has correction plus change (record_cleaning.py:493-496). The agent's second call revised DQ-013 with no correction and was never refused. The padding came from SKILL.md:69, which says without condition "With no affected finding, add "findings": "none: stale listed no finding reading <view>"", even though step 3 says to skip `stale` when no view changed. So the padding is a wording issue in the release, not script enforcement and not the harness.

3) Raw and canonical rows (taxi-A) come mostly from the agent's choices. Codex chose to scan both the raw acquisition (yellow-trips-raw) and the canonical view (yellow-trips-canonical), and passed decisions for every issue in each, extremes included. SKILL.md says the dataset is "usually the canonical view" and to record not-issues and investigation-local extremes only when worth knowing. The script adds rows only for issues it is given. The release has no way to link one issue to several scans, but the bloat itself was the agent's doing, not something the release forced or the harness caused.

The core defect is a real product limitation that a normal interactive user would meet. Medium confidence because the bundled sub-claims are weaker than stated.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-clean/scripts/record_cleaning.py:19-20 (a quality-ID key "revises only judgment cells, keeps the observation and link"); record_cleaning.py:410-425 (a new entry is matched by object+observation, so changed text makes a new row); record_cleaning.py:466-469 (a quality-ID key sets judgment cells only); awb-clean/SKILL.md:69 ("the observation stays as first written"; "With no affected finding, add findings..." with no condition); record_cleaning.py:493-496 (findings required only with a correction, which contradicts the "required" claim)

verdicts.reasoning:
Only the first of the finding's three claims holds up fully.

1) Observations cannot be amended. This is true, and the release causes it. The helper revises only judgment cells. Re-running a `new` entry with corrected text adds a second row rather than changing the first. The skill and template say nothing about correcting, withdrawing or superseding an observation. co2-B confirms the effect. The agent recorded DQ-008 in agent-006 with "so World omits them too". After the user challenged that, the agent revised DQ-008 by quality ID in agent-007. The final quality.md still shows the withdrawn inference in the Observation column; the correction appears only as a note under Current treatment. Earlier, in agent-002, the agent fixed the Libya wording by editing the file directly (a Python string replace). That edit worked, and nothing in the release forbids it. So a workaround exists, but the release never mentions it, and its phrase "stays as first written" reads like a rule. A real user whose observation later turns out wrong would hit this.

2) "clean-record requires a findings string even when no view changed." The helper does not require it. It checks for findings only when a decision includes a correction. Without one, the top-level findings text is never written anywhere, so it cannot pad ledger entries. What does push agents to add it is the skill's own instruction, "With no affected finding, add "findings": "none: stale listed no finding reading <view>"". That instruction has no condition attached, even though step 3 says to skip `stale` when no view changed. In taxi-B, agent-003's second call and agent-005's call sent findings strings with no correction (for example "none: no view changed"). They were harmless and unused. This is a small wording problem in the skill. The entries were not padded.

3) Raw and canonical duplicates in taxi-A (DQ-007 to DQ-025). The agent caused this. It ran two scans of the same data under separate names (`--name yellow-trips-raw` on the landed files, `--name yellow-trips-canonical` on the view). It then recorded every issue from both, including investigation-local extremes. The skill says to work on one dataset at a time, that the dataset is usually the canonical view, and to decide only issues in scope. It makes recording investigation-local properties optional. The helper does lack a way to link a canonical-scan issue to an existing raw-scan row: its marker check refuses that and says to pass the original scan. That gap is real but secondary.

Citation errors in the finding:
- taxi-A-20 is actually about source-register syntax; the matching finding is taxi-A-18.
- taxi-B-41 is not an ID in findings.json; the real evidence is agent-notes.md line 35 and the agent-003 relay call.

Overall: a real but minor product gap (no supported way to amend an observation), with two weaker add-on claims.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-clean/SKILL.md:69 ("Reopening updates judgment cells and the link; the observation stays as first written. A decision on a recorded issue ... revises judgment cells while keeping the observation and link"; also the unconditional "With no affected finding, add "findings": ..."). awb-clean/scripts/record_cleaning.py:19-21 (docstring: a quality-ID key "revises only judgment cells, keeps the observation and link"), :411-424 (a `new` entry matches its row by object plus observation, so different text creates another row), :466-469 (quality-ID branch sets only judgment cells), :493-496 (findings required only when a correction is given; default_findings is used nowhere else), :356-359 (refuses to revise a row recorded from another scan). awb-clean/SKILL.md:8,17,23 (one dataset at a time, usually the canonical view; decide only in-scope issues). Run evidence: co2-B/project/foundation/quality.md DQ-008; co2-B/relay/agent-002.jsonl (Libya fixed by string replace), agent-006.jsonl and agent-007.jsonl (DQ-008 recorded, then revised by quality ID); taxi-B/relay/agent-003.jsonl and agent-005.jsonl (findings strings sent with no correction); taxi-A/relay/agent-002.jsonl (two clean-scan calls named yellow-trips-raw and yellow-trips-canonical).

consolidated.title: Unclear who records the README storage lines when the user names them at setup
consolidated.description: awb-init does not say to fill the README's 'Landed data is kept at' and 'Released packages are kept at' lines when the user names locations up front, and awb-release owns recording release storage. Agents filled the lines with sed at init and were unsure of the expected form. Oct 15 taxi-B reported recording them by hand with no helper.
consolidated.oct15_ref: Oct 15 per-run taxi-B agent.md item 9 (storage locations recorded by hand)
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-38. retail-B-27: compound sed in agent-001. co2-B-22.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to pin this on the harness and couldn't. The release itself is the cause. One severity caveat is below.

1. The harness did not create the trigger. In taxi-B, retail-B and co2-B, the first message (relay/agent-001.in.md) names both storage folders inside the awb-init request. That looks like the persona front-loading answers, and taxi-B-32 tags it that way. But the release README tells users to do exactly this. Its quick-start example at README.md:46 puts both storage paths in the awb-init request. README.md:64 says naming them in the first message saves the question. taxi-B's human/feedback.md:23 says the persona adapted that example. A real user following the README sends the same message.

2. The gap is in the release text. awb-init/SKILL.md never mentions storage or the 'kept at' lines (grep finds 0 matches). Step 3.1 only says to adapt the README template, which ships with both lines set to 'not yet recorded'. The instructions that do own these lines are read at later stages:
- workbench-guides/data.md:27 covers the landed line, 'before the first landing'.
- awb-release/SKILL.md:14 and :47 cover the release line.
Both say to record a location whenever the user gives one, but neither is in front of the agent at init. Nothing documents what form the value should take. Yet awb_landing.py:871 treats any value not starting with '/', '~', './' or '../' as prose and skips retention. So the 'unsure of the form' worry (retail-B agent-notes.md:10) points at a real, undocumented rule.

3. Harness factors ruled out:
- The sandbox and non-interactive mode don't matter here, because the user had already supplied the paths and the agent had nothing to ask.
- Auto-approved MCP tools don't matter either: no helper exists for setting these lines.
- The friction-log note only made the agent's doubt visible; it didn't create it.

All three agents independently filled the lines by hand at init:
- taxi-B and retail-B with a sed one-liner in agent-001.jsonl.
- co2-B with a Python string replace.
Each separately logged that ownership was unclear (taxi-B agent.md:29 and agent-notes.md:8; retail-B agent.md:37 and agent-notes.md:10; co2-B agent-notes.md:7 and agent.md:48).

Caveats:
- No user-facing harm. All six runs, including the A runs, recorded correct absolute paths, and land/retain/release then worked. So this is agent-side instruction friction, minor as filed.
- The cited evidence IDs don't match. taxi-B findings.json has only 35 entries, so taxi-B-38 doesn't exist. retail-B-27 is about duplicate rows in awb-clean. co2-B-22 lists other instruction conflicts, not the storage lines. I confirmed the finding from the agent notes and relay logs directly, not from those IDs.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/SKILL.md:26-37 (step 3 never mentions storage or the 'kept at' lines; 0 grep hits); awb-init/assets/workbench/README.md:9,11 (lines ship as 'not yet recorded'); README.md:46,64 (quick-start tells users to name storage folders in the awb-init message); awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md:27 and awb-release/SKILL.md:14,47 (ownership sits with later stages); awb-init/assets/awb_landing.py:871 (an unwritten rule on the value's form)

verdicts.reasoning:
The gap is real and comes from the release. But it caused agent hesitation only, not a wrong result.

What the release does:
- The user-facing README (README.md:64) tells users to put both storage locations in their first message ("Naming them in your first message usually saves the question within that session").
- awb-init handles that first message, but awb-init/SKILL.md never mentions the 'Landed data is kept at' or 'Released packages are kept at' lines. Its README template ships both lines as 'not yet recorded' (awb-init/assets/workbench/README.md:9,11).
- The rule "Record a location whenever the user provides one" exists in only two places: the data guide (workbench-guides/data.md:27), which AGENTS.md says to read before landing data, and awb-release/SKILL.md:14,47, which loads only at release time. awb-release also owns "record where releases are kept" in its description.
- No helper writes either line. Both the data guide and awb-release expect the line to be edited by hand. Neither says what form the value should take beyond "write the user's answer". The parsers accept absolute, ~, ./ and trailing-slash forms (awb_landing.py:853-878, awb_draft.py:4015ff), so the form doubt has no practical effect.

What the run evidence shows:
- All three B runs met this in turn 1 and each worked out for itself what to do.
  - taxi-B: agent-notes.md:8 and agent.md:29 say it was unclear whether init or awb-release owns the lines. It used a compound sed in relay/agent-001.jsonl.
  - retail-B: agent-notes.md:10 and agent.md:37 say awb-init does not say to fill the lines. It used a compound sed and was "Unsure if retain expects a particular form (trailing slash, absolute path)". That compound call raised the run's one permission prompt (orchestrator-report.md:20).
  - co2-B: agent-notes.md:7 says it "had to infer". It used Python str.replace, not sed, so the finding's "with sed" holds for two runs, not three.
- In every run, all six A and B included, the lines ended up correctly recorded as absolute paths. Retention and release copies worked (retail-B notes "both storage paths reachable"; co2-B notes land/retain copied to storage automatically).
- So the impact is agent uncertainty plus hand edits. No user saw anything wrong, which fits severity minor.
- This is not a harness artifact. The persona did front-load the paths, but the release's own README asks users to do exactly that.

Citation problems in the finding:
- taxi-B-38 does not exist; taxi-B findings.json has 35 entries.
- retail-B-27 is about awb-clean duplicate rows. The storage-line finding is retail-B-21, and the compound-call prompt is retail-B-30.
- co2-B-22 lists other instruction conflicts and does not mention the storage lines.
- The underlying feedback files do support the finding.
- The "Oct 15 taxi-B" claim could not be checked from these folders.
verdicts.release_evidence: README.md:64 (invites naming storage in the first message); awb-init/SKILL.md (no mention of either storage line anywhere); awb-init/assets/workbench/README.md:9,11 (lines ship as 'not yet recorded'); awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md:27 and awb-release/SKILL.md:14,47 (the only 'record whenever the user names one' rules, outside init's flow, hand-edit with no form spec)

consolidated.title: Long, repetitive replies from stacked Codex commentary
consolidated.description: Codex-agent replies repeated content (the four scope questions twice in reply 1; confirmation asked twice) and opened with progress narration ('I'm finishing...'). The relay joins every interim agent_message to the final one, where an interactive host would stream them as progress, so part of the length is a relay effect. The rest is reply style that the skills neither require nor forbid.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-13: transcript lines 31-45 vs 55-60; agent-001.out.md vs .last.md. co2-A-17: agent-004.out.md vs .last.md. retail-A-25: A1, A6.

verdicts.reasoning:
Almost all the repetition the simulated users complained about comes from the harness. The release did not cause it.

1) The doubled scope questions in taxi-A reply 1 and retail-A A1 are not two pieces of text the agent wrote. The first copy is a `request_user_input_async` call: Codex's structured multiple-choice question tool. The evidence is in the taxi-A rollout (rollout-...01a14625-951a...jsonl, ordinal 54, call; ordinal 55, the same content as an AgentMessage) and the retail-A rollout (01a14625-ab9a, ordinal 47). Under non-interactive `codex exec`, the call returned `{"accepted":true}` with no answer, and exec printed it as an `agent_message` item. relay.py `_codex_reply` (kit/relay.py:212) joins every agent_message with the final one. So the question picker turned into a block of text, and the questions, still unanswered, came back in the final message. On an interactive host they would appear as a picker the user can answer mid-turn.

2) The progress narration ("I'm finishing the package checks...") is in the `commentary` phase in every cited turn. This holds for all 5 interim messages in co2-A agent-004 and the interim messages in retail-A A6, checked against each rollout's phase field. Codex's own base instructions say commentary messages "are collapsed after the final answer is shown to users" and that "the final answer must always be fully self-contained". So on a real Codex host the final message restating things is intended behaviour, and the interim messages are progress updates. They only look like one long reply because the relay stacked them. co2-A agent-004.last.md, the real reply, is concise and has no repetition.

3) What remains inside a final message is the second confirm in retail-A A6. The last.md asks "Confirm these changes" in bold, then adds a paragraph quoting awb-package's "wait for their yes". That quote paragraph comes from a Codex base-instruction rule: "If a skill causes you to ask for permission or confirmation, pause... name and link to the exact SKILL.md you read, quote the relevant instruction". It does not come from the release. The release's AGENTS.md:30 actually says the opposite: "never send them to a skill or instruction file". This part is real Codex host behaviour, but the host prompt causes it, not the release. It is also the skill-quoting issue, not stacked commentary.

The release asks for the interview round once, "in this report" (awb-init/SKILL.md:46), and asks for a single plain question per message (AGENTS.md:30). Nothing in it causes interim messages or repetition. The finding's own claim that the skills "neither require nor forbid" the reply style is too generous: the release asks for a single ask. Because the real cause is the relay plus exec's rendering of the question tool, the verdict is harness.
verdicts.release_evidence: No release file causes this, and the release text points the other way. awb-init/SKILL.md:46 asks for the first interview round once, "asking it in this report". awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:30 says "ask in that message ... never send them to a skill or instruction file". The causes are all outside the release. In the harness: kit/relay.py:212 (`"\n\n".join(texts)` over every agent_message). In the run logs: taxi-A rollout ordinals 54-57 (request_user_input_async rendered as an AgentMessage, output {"accepted":true}) and retail-A rollout ordinal 47 (the same pattern). In the Codex host's base instructions: the rule that commentary is "collapsed after the final answer", and the rule to quote SKILL.md on skill-caused pauses.

verdicts.reasoning:
Nearly all of the extra length is a relay artifact. The release does not cause it.

1. The relay builds each reply by joining every agent_message from the codex exec stream (kit/relay.py:196-212). The Codex rollouts tag each of those messages with a phase. The interim narration is phase=commentary in every case: "I'm using awb-init…" and "I'm finishing the sensitivity checks…" in taxi-A, and "…I'm finishing the package checks and file index" in co2-A agent-004. Codex's own preamble behaviour produces these. An interactive host streams them as live progress next to the tool calls. Every final_answer (.last.md) in taxi-A, co2-A and retail-A opens with substance, never narration.

2. In taxi-A A1 and retail-A A1, the first copy of the four scope questions is not a chat message. It is a call to the host's native `request_user_input_async` tool, which returned {"accepted":true} (taxi-A rollout 15-17-11, line 55). codex exec rendered that call as a text AgentMessage, and the relay then joined it to the final answer. On an interactive Codex host it would appear as a question prompt with options, not as a block of text. The final answer asks the questions once, as the release directs: awb-init/SKILL.md:46 says to ask the first interview round "in this report", and AGENTS.md:30 says "ask in that message". On a host with that tool, the final message would add a short pointer to the questions. That is a mild recap, not repeated content.

3. co2-A agent-004's .last.md contains no repetition. Everything extra in out.md is concatenated commentary.

4. retail-A A6's .last.md asks for confirmation once. The second line is "I'm waiting at your requested show-first checkpoint; awb-package requires '…wait for their yes'", which quotes a skill file. taxi-A A1 does the same ("The awb-init instructions require…"). The release already forbids this: AGENTS.md:30 says "never send them to a skill or instruction file". So that part of the length comes from the agent ignoring a clear instruction (already logged separately as retail-A finding #6), not from a gap in the release.

The finding itself attributes the remainder to "reply style that the skills neither require nor forbid". No shipped instruction, helper or template causes the progress narration or the duplicate questions.
verdicts.release_evidence: No release text causes it. kit/relay.py:196-212 (harness, not release) joins every agent_message. awb-init/SKILL.md:46 says to ask the interview round "in this report" (once). awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:30 says "ask in that message … never send them to a skill or instruction file", which the agent broke when it quoted skill files. The first copy of the questions is the host tool call `request_user_input_async`, at taxi-A/agent-home/.codex/sessions/2026/10/16/rollout-2026-10-16T15-17-11-…jsonl line 55.

consolidated.title: Chat-only figures change base, contradict themselves or are misstated
consolidated.description: No check covers chat replies, and their figures slipped. Denominators switched without notice: the code-0 share was 6.9% of all records, then 4.02% and 8.85% of screened trips; qualifying zones went from 54 to 53; the cash-tip share went 0.03%, 0.04%, then 0.01%. Hours within ±5% were called 'exceptions'. February and April were called the low points when April was only fifth-lowest. Coded entities were miscounted (219 instead of 218 plus Kosovo). Most were corrected in the next turn or caught in the draft.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-18: replies 2-4; msgs 4 and 5. taxi-B-19: reply 4. retail-B-41: A2 section 1 vs the A3 table; reviewer pass 1. co2-B-25: A2 vs A3.

verdicts.reasoning:
I couldn't pin these slips on the harness.

1. The relay didn't change anything. relay/agent-00N.out.md matches transcript.md word for word on every disputed figure. This includes "6.9%" and "0.04%" in agent-002, "54 zones qualify" and "0.01% or fewer" in agent-003, and "53 zones" and "The exceptions:" in agent-004.

2. The agent kept its context the whole time. All of taxi-B's agent turns ran in one resumed session, 58390a06…, and none of the agent jsonl files in taxi-B, retail-B or co2-B contains a compact_boundary event. Lost memory between turns doesn't explain the switching bases.

3. Nothing in the harness pushes toward this. The agent system prompt says "Behave exactly as you normally would". The friction-log note adds a side task but doesn't touch how the agent reports figures. The sandbox, the simulated home folder and MCP auto-approval play no part in how a reply states its numbers.

4. The slips come from the agent's own queries. Reply 1 took a first look at raw files. Reply 2 counted all records: 419,151 of 6,041,527 is 6.94%, and 324 of 893,768 is 0.04%. Reply 3 used screened trips: 4.02%, 8.85% and 0.01%. No reply said the base had changed. The "54 zones" figure came from an ad-hoc `awb.py sql` count over all of yellow_trips, grouped by PULocationID. That count included the unknown zone and skipped screening, while the ranking it described had 53 zones. Reply 4 calls hours at −1% to −4.5% "exceptions" to a ±5% band. In co2-B, A2 says "219 entities with a code, plus Kosovo" and A3 says "219 included entries". In retail-B, the table in A3 shows April 2010 as only the fifth-lowest month of year one.

5. The persona did no front-loading here. The figures drifted between turns on their own. The Codex persona's checking is the reason anyone caught the slips; a less careful real user would be more likely to take them as given. That makes the product concern stronger, not weaker.

Why I count it as product: the release checks numbers only in recorded findings (the `state finding` warning) and in drafts (check-draft). AGENTS.md says nothing about stating the base of a share in chat, or flagging a base change. It does say ad-hoc query output is exploration, but it doesn't say how chat should label it. So nothing a real user would run stops these slips. The co2-B referee reached the same tag: "nothing on the host prevents it."

Why confidence is only medium:
- The errors themselves are model slips. The release only fails to guard against them.
- The finding's "chat-only" label is partly wrong for retail-B. Its "February and April are the troughs" wording was also written into the recorded finding text through `state finding`. That check passed it because the index values 68.9 and 61.7 do exist in the result, even though the claim is semantically wrong. The draft review caught it later.
- Three of the cited evidence IDs don't match the runs' findings.json files. taxi-B-18 is about the TOML template, taxi-B-19 is about the p1.partial directory, and retail-B has only 35 findings, so retail-B-41 doesn't exist. Only co2-B-25 matches. The underlying facts can still be checked in the transcripts.
verdicts.release_evidence:
These files are under release/analytics-workbench-skills.
- awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:26-32: the Conversation section has no rule about the base of a chat figure, about where a chat figure must come from, or about flagging a base change.
- AGENTS.md:40: query output from outside run.py counts as exploration, but nothing says how chat should label it.
- awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md:17: the only number check runs on finding text, via the `state finding` warning about unrecorded numbers. Drafts are checked separately by check-draft. Nothing checks chat replies.

verdicts.reasoning:
Most of the transcript evidence holds. I checked it against the run data.

taxi-B:
- Payment code 0 base switch. Reply 2 gave 6.9% as a share of all records: 419,151 / 6,041,527. Reply 3 gave "4.02% of trips in January and 8.85% in July" without naming the base. Those are shares of screened-in trips (payment-mix.csv share_of_valid_trips 0.0402 / 0.0885). The user asked about it in msg 4, and reply 4 explained it with a table.
- Zone count. Reply 3 said "54 zones qualify" and reply 4 said 53. zone-count-check.csv shows 54 counted unknown zone 264/265. The user raised it in msg 5, and reply 5 explained it.
- Cash-tip share. It went 0.03% (reply 1, raw peek), then 0.04% (reply 2, 324 / 893,768 = 0.036% of all records), then "0.01% or fewer" (reply 3, screened-in July, payment-mix 0.0001).
- "Exceptions" mislabel. Reply 4 listed "-1% to -4.5%" hours as exceptions to "within ±5%". volume-by-hour.csv confirms 2 a.m. is -1.1% and 3 a.m. is -4.5%.

co2-B: A2 said "219 entities with a code, plus Kosovo". I counted the OWID CSV myself: 218 coded entities, and Kosovo's iso_code is blank. quality.md DQ-004 and A3 correctly say 219 in total, so the error is in chat only.

Two problems with the finding's evidence:
- **retail-B is mis-cited.** "February and April are the troughs" is not a chat-only figure. It is in the recorded finding (state.md line 9 and findings.json, still supported), and is defensible there as each year's lowest month (index 68.9 for Feb 2010, 61.7 for Apr 2011). The reviewer caught it in the draft, not in chat: findings.md:23 "only the fifth-lowest month of year one". The agent's fix then over-corrected to "February was lowest in both years", and it caught that itself. This item supports "caught in the draft", not "chat figures slipped".
- **The cited IDs don't match the findings files.** findings.json taxi-B-18/19 are about TOML parsing and the leftover p1.partial directory, and retail-B has no finding 41 (it has 35). Only co2-B-25 matches. The transcript content behind the taxi-B citations does match.

Release cause. No shipped instruction covers figures in chat replies, and no check does either. The guard is absent rather than being an instruction that causes the errors:
- The number-trace checks cover only finding text (`state finding` warns on unrecorded numbers, analysis.md:17) and package files (check-draft, README.md:112).
- The AGENTS.md Conversation section (lines 26-32) says nothing about where chat numbers come from, keeping a base consistent, or naming the denominator.
- AGENTS.md:40 only says to present non-run.py output "as exploration". That does not stop a base switch or a paraphrase slip such as "219 with a code".
- README.md:5 tells users the agent "answers your questions with numbers it records and checks". Users approve findings on the strength of the figures in chat replies (taxi-B msg 5 "I accept the five descriptive answers"; retail-B msg 4).

The slips themselves are ordinary model errors, and the simulation setup played no part in them. A real interactive user would see the same unguarded chat figures. Severity is minor: most were corrected the next turn, often because the persona asked, or caught in the draft.
verdicts.release_evidence:
The release has no instruction that causes these errors, and none that prevents them; the gap is the cause.
- awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:26-32 (Conversation section: no rule on where chat figures come from or on stating their base).
- AGENTS.md:40 (only says non-run.py output is presented "as exploration").
- awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md:17 (number warning applies to `state finding` text only).
- README.md:112 (package check covers findings.md, methodology and methods note only).
- README.md:5 (promises the agent "answers your questions with numbers it records and checks", which nothing enforces for chat).

consolidated.title: Status counts findings against the user's questions without mapping them
consolidated.description: The footer and status now count the user's own questions, but awb-status still reports finding counts ('Nine findings are supported', '11 supported findings') against five questions. The footer named no question ('1 answered'), and a question the agent added became a sixth root. Users had to guess how the numbers relate.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-11: transcript lines 111, 118 and 178; AGENTS.md line 32; awb-status SKILL line 27. retail-A-07: A4; human notes turn 5.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not tie the core behaviour to the simulation setup. It comes from release text that any interactive host would load.

(1) Finding counts in awb-status. In taxi-A turn 4, the status collector returned active.counts {"supported":9,"superseded":1} (relay/agent-004.jsonl). awb-status/SKILL.md line 27 says to report active.counts. Line 28 says to report the roots as "Your five questions: 5 of 5 answered". Nothing tells the agent how findings relate to those questions. The agent did what both lines say: "Nine findings are supported" sat next to "All five study answers are accepted". retail-A turn 4 shows the same pattern in a separate Codex session on a different dataset: "11 supported findings ... All five original questions and their required follow-ups are answered." The README never says that one question can produce several findings: line 83 says each answer "is recorded as a finding" and line 98 defines a finding. Both personas noted the gap on their own (taxi-A notes turn 5; retail-A notes turn 5).

(2) The footer named no question. The awb-init AGENTS.md template, line 32, gives a count-only example ("Your five questions: 3 answered, 2 open"). The agent's footer "1 answered, 4 open" followed it, and the persona had to ask which question that was (transcript line 118). The relay is faithful: agent-002.last.md and agent-004.last.md match the transcript.

Harness causes I checked and ruled out:
- Non-interactive exec or the sandbox: status output and footers would read the same in an interactive session.
- Auto-approved MCP: it changes nothing about what gets reported.
- The harness note on message 1: it only asks for a private log.
- Persona front-loading: the confusion arose mid-run, from output the agent produced.
- Relay mistakes: none found.

Caveats that weaken the finding without moving it to harness:
- Both personas guessed the mapping correctly and called it only "a little/a bit confusing", so minor is the right severity.
- The "sixth root" part was never visible to the user. The collector counted Vendor 6 (Q-009, recorded with no parent because the user asked about it) as a sixth root, but the agent noticed in its reasoning and wrote "five study questions ... TLC follow-ups: 2 open". That sub-claim is an agent-side observation, and the finding's wording that the agent added the question is loose.
- retail-A-07 in that run's findings.json is about clean/explore steps, so that evidence ID is mislabelled. The cited human notes turn 5 does support the claim.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-status/SKILL.md:27 (report active.counts, the finding counts) together with awb-status/SKILL.md:28 (lead with roots, "Your five questions: 5 of 5 answered"), with no instruction mapping findings to questions; awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:32 (footer example counts answered/open and names no question); awb-status/scripts/collect_status.py:132-133 (roots = all parentless questions) and :226 (active.counts = finding status counts); README.md:83 and :98 (findings defined, but nothing saying one question can produce several)

verdicts.reasoning:
The core of the finding holds and comes from the release. Part of it is overstated, and one citation is wrong.

1. **Footer without question names (taxi-A).** Transcript line 111 shows the footer as "Your five questions: 1 answered, 4 open". At line 118 the user had to ask whether that meant Q4. This follows the shipped template. awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:32 tells the agent to end a turn with a count of the ledger's roots and gives the example "Your five questions: 3 answered, 2 open". README.md:108 describes the same footer. No shipped file tells the agent to say which questions changed status. The agent followed the template as written.

2. **Finding counts reported against question counts (both runs).** awb-status/SKILL.md:27 tells the agent to report `active.counts`, the finding counts by status. Line 28 then tells it to lead with the user's questions, the roots. Nothing tells the agent to relate findings to questions. The README never explains it either. README.md:98 defines "Finding" and :100 defines "Question ledger", but neither says that one question can produce several findings.
   - In taxi-A, status said "Nine findings are supported" (transcript line 178) beside five accepted answers. The user ranked this as pain point 4 in feedback/human.md:14 and :24.
   - In retail-A, status (A4) said "11 supported findings". human/notes.md:41 calls it "a bit confusing, but presumably it includes the follow-ups". So that user worked it out, and the agent had added "All five original questions and their required follow-ups are answered", which partly explains the gap. retail-A is weaker support.

3. **Overstated: the "sixth root".** The user asked the Vendor 6 question in chat ("what is Vendor 6?" ... "I'll note it as a question for the TLC"). The release defines a root as a question the user asked (CHANGELOG.md:105, awb-init/references/provenance.md:21), so recording Q-009 as a root fits that rule. The user never saw a six-question count. The agent's footers and status split the counts ("Your five study questions: 5 answered · TLC follow-ups: 2 open"). That complaint comes only from the agent's own feedback (feedback/agent.md:34), not from anything the user hit.

4. **Wrong citation.** retail-A-07 in retail-A/feedback/findings.json is about clean and explore being folded into analysis, not about counts. The A4 and notes Turn 5 evidence that C-48 points to does exist and supports a mild version of the claim.

Net: a real user on a normal host would get the same opaque "1 answered" footer and an unexplained findings-versus-questions count. Both come directly from the shipped footer template and the status report order. It stays minor: no turn was wasted on it alone, since the taxi-A user bundled the question with two other requests.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:32 (footer counts roots, example "Your five questions: 3 answered, 2 open", no instruction to name which questions); awb-status/SKILL.md:27 (report active.counts finding totals) and :28 (lead with roots), with no guidance relating findings to questions; README.md:98, :100 and :108 (define finding and ledger and describe the footer, but never explain how findings map to questions). Counter-evidence for the "sixth root" part: CHANGELOG.md:105 and awb-init/references/provenance.md:21 (a question the user asks is a root, so Q-009 was recorded correctly).

consolidated.title: Counting the title and fixed slides still confuses the requested slide count
consolidated.description: #61 added an appendix, a one-sentence statement that the deck opens with the title slide and then the Answer slide, and slide counts that include the title. In taxi-A, the preview's 'the deck opens with the title, then the answer slide', with the title counted as slide 1, took the user a moment to map, and the '8-slide' deck held 7 content slides. In retail-A, the required structure gave nine slides against 'about 8', which the agent settled as 8 main slides plus an appendix.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-14: transcript line 201; awb-package SKILL line 52. retail-A-11: headline preview in A2; findings-template required slides.

verdicts.reasoning:
Neither run shows a user confused about the requested slide count, and both decks came out the way the user asked.

taxi-A: The release does tell the agent what to say. awb-package/SKILL.md line 52 says to state in one sentence that the deck opens with a title slide and then the answer slide, and to count the title among the main slides. The agent followed that and was explicit about it. Transcript line 201: "8 main slides, including the title, plus 4 appendix reference slides. The deck opens with the title, then the answer slide." The only user-side evidence is human/notes.md line 43: the list numbers the title as slide 1, which "Took a second to map." That is a brief pause over how the list is numbered, not confusion about the count against the request. The persona's later summary (findings.json taxi-A-13) says the preview counted the title "without saying so", which is wrong: the agent did say so. So the user-side signal is a misreading by the simulated persona, which was told to log every bit of friction. The claim that the "8-slide" deck "held 7 content slides" is the finding author's own reading. The user asked for "about 8 slides", accepted the 8 main + 4 appendix plan, and never raised the count again.

retail-A: Nothing from the user. human/notes.md does not mention slide counting. human/feedback.md line 5 says "I have an 8-slide outline" and treats it as a success. The "nine slides against about 8" point comes only from the agent's own notes (agent.md 1.6; agent-notes.md line 35). The required structure (title, Answer, five findings, How we know, Limitations) gives 9. The agent did what SKILL.md line 52 and findings-template.md line 12 describe: it reported the count and proposed moving Limitations to the appendix. The user accepted. The release's own length mechanism worked as designed, so there was no confusion.

On the harness question: the faint taxi-A signal does lean toward harness. It comes from the simulated human's role behaviour: logging a split-second pause, then misremembering it. The relay also passed through Codex's interim narration ("starting with the two decisions"), though an interactive Codex host would show that too. Still, the core problem is that the evidence does not show the claimed confusion, not that the harness caused it. So the verdict is unsupported rather than harness.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/SKILL.md:52 tells the agent to state that the deck opens with the title and then the Answer slide, to count the title among the main slides, and to propose appendix moves when the count runs over. awb-package/assets/package-format/findings-template.md:12 lists the required slides. Contradicting evidence: taxi-A transcript.md:201 shows the agent said "8 main slides, including the title". retail-A human/feedback.md:5 says "I have an 8-slide outline" with no complaint. The only user friction is taxi-A human/notes.md:43, "Took a second to map".

verdicts.reasoning:
The runs don't show users getting confused about slide counts, and they don't show the release causing it. In both runs the agent did exactly what the release says, and the user accepted the count without a problem.

What the release says:
- awb-package/SKILL.md:52 tells the agent to "say in one sentence that the deck opens with a title slide and then the answer slide." It also says to "Report the main slides, title included, and the appendix slides against any recorded length," and to propose appendix moves when the main slides exceed that length.
- findings-template.md:12 lists the required slides. Line 104 makes the Appendix the place for slides that would take the deck past the recorded length.

taxi-A:
- At transcript line 201 the agent says "8 main slides, including the title, plus 4 appendix reference slides. The deck opens with the title, then the answer slide." It then numbers the title as item 1. That is the SKILL wording to the letter.
- The cited taxi-A finding (taxi-A-13; the ID given, taxi-A-14, is an unrelated settings.toml finding) says the title was counted "without saying so." Line 201 contradicts that.
- The only sign of confusion is one line in human/notes.md turn 6: "Took a second to map." The user's next message (message 6) correctly referred to slides 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8.
- The user's final feedback.md lists no slide-count or title problem among its pain points.
- The deck having 7 content slides out of "8" follows from the stated rule. The user never objected to it.

retail-A:
- The cited finding is retail-A-10; the ID given, retail-A-11, is an unrelated UCI-wording finding.
- The required slides (title, answer, five findings, How we know, Limitations) came to nine against "about 8." The agent did what SKILL:52 and template:104 prescribe: 8 main slides plus Limitations in the appendix, stated in the preview.
- The user accepted without comment and later wrote "I have an 8-slide outline." The human files show no confusion.
- The agent's own feedback (agent.md item 6) is a design suggestion, such as allowing slides to be combined. It is not evidence that a user was confused.

What remains is a matter of taste: the preview listed the title in the same bold, numbered format as the headlines. That is the agent's formatting, not something the release requires. It caused a moment's pause in one run and no wrong outcome.
verdicts.release_evidence: These release lines prevent the problem rather than cause it: awb-package/SKILL.md:52 (opening-sentence rule, main slides counted with the title, propose appendix moves when over length), awb-package/assets/package-format/findings-template.md:12 (required slides; deck opens with the title slide, then Answer) and :104 (Appendix holds slides past the recorded length), README.md:70 (slide count reported against length, extra slides proposed for the appendix). Run evidence: taxi-A/transcript.md:201 (title counted and said so), taxi-A/human/notes.md:43 ("took a second to map"), retail-A/transcript.md:101-112, retail-A/feedback/human.md:5 ("8-slide outline").

consolidated.title: START-HERE lists methodology.md and deck-rules.md both as files to attach and as internal files not to send
consolidated.description: The START-HERE generator added in #64 puts the builder attach list, which includes methodology.md and deck-rules.md, in part 2, and lists the same files as internal in part 3. Users found this confusing, and co2-A's release still lists both files in both places after the agent's fix.
consolidated.evidence: co2-A-13: awb_draft.py start_here(); released 001/START-HERE.md; U5 item 4. retail-A-14: released 001/START-HERE.md parts 2 and 3.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and found none. The text comes straight from the release and is the same every time it is generated.

1. **The release builds the contradiction into the file.** `start_here()` in the released awb_draft.py lists methodology.md and deck-rules.md in part 2's attach list. Part 3 then lists the same two files under the heading "Internal: keep these, and do not send them", with no "to the audience" qualifier. The only hint that the two parts mean different things is the closing line ("The other files in part 2 are the deck's source"), which leaves it to the reader to work out that "other" means files not in part 3.

2. **retail-A used the release code unchanged.** Its project copy at src/packaging/draft.py has the same sha256 (a8cc2957…) as the release's awb_draft.py. Its draft and both released copies of START-HERE.md (project released/001 and storage/releases/…/001) match the generator's output exactly. The persona flagged it on its own, without prompting: human/notes.md Turn 6 line 54, Overall item 7, and feedback/human.md line 73. Its words were "slightly confusing… clear on a second read".

3. **co2-A shows the same thing.** The persona asked the agent to clarify START-HERE (transcript line 283, U5 item 4). The agent then edited its project copy of draft.py: the diff against the release adds "to the audience" and one sentence saying the builder may read methodology.md. Both files still appear in both lists. The user had asked only for a one-line clarification, so "still lists both after the fix" is weak supporting evidence. It shows that the agent clarified the wording and kept the double listing.

**Harness causes I checked:**
- **Non-interactive exec, Codex sandbox, auto-approved MCP, simulated home folder:** none affects what a deterministic text generator writes.
- **Relay:** both personas opened START-HERE.md from disk, so nothing was paraphrased.
- **Persona front-loading:** neither persona's brief mentions START-HERE.
- **Persona behaviour:** the personas were told to notice confusion, which may make them more sensitive. But the confusing text itself is the release's, and two separate runs reacted to it the same way.

**What argues against a bigger finding:**
- The product README (line 15) says the builder may consult methodology.md and the audience does not get it.
- Both users worked out the meaning on their own.

The package is still meant to be read on its own (the code comment says START-HERE exists "so whoever holds the package or a release knows which files go"). Anyone who receives a release folder without the README would hit the same apparent conflict. Minor severity is right.

The finding's evidence IDs (co2-A-13, retail-A-14) point at unrelated reply-style findings in the runs' findings.json. The matching findings are co2-A-11 and retail-A-19, and the underlying files support those.
verdicts.release_evidence: release/analytics-workbench-skills/awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:2596-2611 (attach list includes "methodology.md", "deck-rules.md"; part 3 heading "3. Internal: keep these, and do not send them" lists the same files). Confirmed unmodified in retail-A (same sha256 for project/src/packaging/draft.py), which produced storage/releases/marketing-investment/leadership-budget/001/START-HERE.md with both files in parts 2 and 3. README.md:15 says the builder may read methodology.md, but START-HERE does not carry that line.

verdicts.reasoning:
The shipped generator causes this. In release awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py, start_here() builds the part 2 attach list as findings.md, each chart, "methodology.md", "deck-rules.md" and assembly/m365.md. Part 3 is then hard-coded as "3. Internal: keep these, and do not send them" and lists methodology.md, manifest.json and deck-rules.md. The heading does not say who the files must not go to, so it reads as contradicting part 2's "attach these files". The only clarification is the generic last line ("The other files in part 2 are the deck's source; your audience gets the deck instead") plus README.md:15, which says the builder may consult methodology.md. The co2-A user called that README note easy to miss. Both helpers.md:34 and package-contract.md:21 specify this double listing, so it is designed behaviour, not agent drift.

The run evidence holds up:
- **retail-A:** the project's src/packaging/draft.py:2606 is unmodified, and released/001/START-HERE.md shows both files in both parts. The simulated user flagged it in human/notes.md:54 and :79 and in feedback/human.md:73 ("Slightly confusing... makes sense on a second read").
- **co2-A:** the user raised it as item 4 of turn U5 (transcript.md:283). The agent's fix was to edit the project copy, src/packaging/draft.py:2620-2621, adding "to the audience" and a sentence saying the builder may read methodology.md. The released START-HERE still lists methodology.md and deck-rules.md in both part 2 and part 3, as the finding says, but the fix softened the confusion there. The user confirmed in feedback/human.md:26 that the fix worked.

Every other run's project code has the same unmodified heading, so any real user reading START-HERE would see it. Severity minor: both users worked out the intended meaning.

consolidated.title: Release folders nest investigation and package names the user never chose or was told
consolidated.description: #64 dropped the 'released' segment from the storage path. Storage still nests names the agent derived (co2-country-priorities/donor-roundtable/001, marketing-investment/leadership-budget/001). The agents did not report the package name as awb-package step 1 requires, and the README explains the layout only in 'How it works'.
consolidated.evidence: co2-A-20: A6. retail-A-13: release path in A7; README 'How it works'.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not tie this finding to how the simulation was run. Every part of it comes from the release, and a real user on an interactive host would hit it.

1) The nested layout comes from the release helper. awb_draft.py builds the copy target as base / investigation / package / number. All six runs, including the B runs with a Claude agent, ended up with <releases>/<investigation>/<package>/001/.

2) Nobody asks the user for the investigation name, and nothing requires reporting it. awb-scope tells the agent to create investigations/<slug>/ with the slug "named for the question". Its Report step does not ask for the slug to be stated. So even an agent that followed every instruction would never tell the user "co2-country-priorities" or "marketing-investment".

3) Package name: awb-package step 1 says to "derive a short, stable one ... and report it". In both A runs the Codex agent did not report it. I searched every completed agent_message in the Codex jsonl logs. The names appear only inside link paths, such as deliveries/co2-country-priorities/donor-roundtable/draft/headline-preview.md, plus co2-A A5's "Mark donor-roundtable delivered". So no message was dropped by the relay. The harness note only said "work exactly as you normally would". By contrast, the Claude agent in co2-B did report its package name ("I'll call it `donor-briefing` unless you prefer another"). That makes this half partly a matter of which model follows the instruction. But Codex is a supported host, and running non-interactively does not explain leaving the name out. Step 7 (Report) also does not repeat the requirement.

4) README: the user's copy of the README is byte-identical to the release README. Its user-facing lines (29, 86) say only that the release is copied "to your release folder". The <location>/<investigation>/<package>/<n>/ layout appears only under 'How it works' (line 137). The generated project README also mentions the layout, again only as an internal path note.

5) Persona front-loading does not change the result. The user named the releases folder up front, so awb-release never asked where releases are kept. But that question would not have explained the nested names either; step 5 reports only where the copy went.

Both simulated users noticed it on their own and rated it minor: co2-A human/notes.md turn 6 and retail-A human/notes.md turn 8 plus feedback/human.md section 3. These match findings co2-A-16 and retail-A-18, not the co2-A-20 and retail-A-13 IDs the finding's evidence line cites. One small overstatement: the user was "never told" only in the sense that the names were never introduced or explained. They did appear in file links from A2 onward.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:4045 (target = base / investigation / package / number); awb-package/SKILL.md:22 ("derive a short, stable one from the investigation and a purpose word and report it"); awb-scope/SKILL.md:55 and :63 (slug derived from the question, with no requirement to report or confirm it); README.md:137 (the only place the layout is described, under 'How it works'), against README.md:29 and :86 ("copies it to your release folder", with no layout)

verdicts.reasoning:
The release causes this, and the run evidence shows it. The cited IDs are wrong, though: the matching findings are co2-A-16 and retail-A-18. co2-A-20 and retail-A-13 are about other things (source registration, and non-product stock codes).

**What happens in the runs**
- Both runs' storage holds the nested folders: co2-A/storage/releases/co2-country-priorities/donor-roundtable/001 and retail-A/storage/releases/marketing-investment/leadership-budget/001.
- In co2-A A6, the release report links into that nested path. In retail-A A7, the agent prints the exact nested folder.
- Both user personas flagged the nesting (co2-A human/notes.md turn 6; retail-A feedback, from U8).
- Neither agent ever reported the package name as a name it had chosen. In co2-A it appears only inside link paths from reply 2 on, plus "Mark donor-roundtable delivered" in A5. In retail-A it appears only inside paths.
- Across all six runs, only co2-B followed awb-package step 1 ("I'll call it `donor-briefing` unless you prefer another"). The other five showed the name only in paths, so this is a pattern across runs, not one agent slipping.

**What the release does**
1. The nesting is designed into the helper: awb_draft.py:4035 builds `{location}/{investigation}/{package}/{number}/`.
2. Nothing tells the user the investigation name. awb-scope SKILL.md:55 creates `investigations/<slug>/` with no instruction to report or confirm the slug.
3. The package-name instruction is weak. awb-package SKILL.md:22 does say "derive a short, stable one ... and report it", but it sits mid-paragraph. The step 7 report list (SKILL.md:91) asks only for "the draft path", which agents can read as covering the name.
4. The README's quick-start text never mentions the nesting. README.md:29 ("What you get") says only "Each release is copied to the folder you name for releases", and README.md:64 does not mention it either. The `<location>/<investigation>/<package>/<n>/` layout appears only in "How it works" (README.md:137).

**Why the verdict is product**
Nothing here depends on the harness. A real user on a normal interactive host would find their release under two agent-chosen folder levels they were never asked about, and the quick-start text would not prepare them for it. Agents did ignore the step 1 instruction, but five of six did, and the investigation slug has no reporting instruction at all, so the release is the cause.

**Caveats on severity**
- "Never told" is a little overstated: the names did appear in the file paths the agents showed throughout, and both release reports gave the location.
- Nesting by investigation and package is a reasonable way to keep releases from colliding.
- Minor severity is right.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:4035 (destination nests {investigation}/{package}/{number}); README.md:29 (says only "copied to the folder you name for releases", no nesting mentioned) versus README.md:137 ("How it works" is the only place the layout appears); awb-scope/SKILL.md:55 (slug created, no instruction to report it); awb-package/SKILL.md:22 ("derive ... and report it", ignored in 5 of 6 runs) and :91 (report list asks only for "the draft path")

consolidated.title: The deck is an outline package, and when to build it relative to release is unclear
consolidated.description: Users now know the package is a Markdown outline plus chart CSVs, not a PPTX; taxi-A's user accepted that, citing the README and START-HERE. co2-A's user could not tell whether to build and review the PowerPoint before or after release. awb-status said 'assemble and review PowerPoint, then Mark donor-roundtable delivered', and the README does not address the order.
consolidated.evidence: co2-A-12: A5 status and footer; U6. taxi-A-25: START-HERE.md; methodology-note.md about 400 words.

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding makes two claims. Neither shows a release defect.

1. The deck is an outline package. This is not a problem in the evidence. taxi-A's user found START-HERE clear and accepted the outline (taxi-A/human/notes.md lines 48-50; feedback/human.md line 45). Its findings.json item taxi-A-23 is an agent note, and its own tag reason says the user accepted it. taxi-A shows no confusion about build order. Its transcript never suggests building the deck before release.

2. Build order relative to release. Only co2-A shows confusion, and its source is the Codex agent's own wording, not the release:
- In turn 5 the agent wrote the next step itself: `awb/records state next --add "Review the corrected donor-roundtable working copy, then assemble and visually check the PowerPoint using START-HERE.md..."` (co2-A/relay/agent-005.jsonl, seen through logview).
- awb-status then repeated that next step from state.md, because collect_status reads the state.md "Next steps" section verbatim.
- The agent also wrote the footer line "next: assemble and review PowerPoint, then Mark delivered". AGENTS.md:32 leaves the footer's next step to the agent.
- Nothing in the release puts deck assembly before release. awb-status's suggestion table offers "Mark the <package> package delivered" whenever a draft has no release, with no assembly step first. START-HERE says "the deck, once you build it". deck-rules' Revision boundary sends any content change back for a refreshed package.
- The agent seems to have stretched the user's "hold off on commits" to cover the release ("No numbered release or commits yet, as requested"). The user never asked to hold the release.
- The README is silent on order, but it did not mislead. The user read it as making the package the deliverable and released correctly (notes.md turn 5: "README implies the package itself is the deliverable... Releasing now").
- After the release, the same agent said "build your PowerPoint from the frozen package". In the other runs, agents said "build the deck from the release" (taxi-B line 580, co2-B line 582) or gave no build-first step.

So one run out of six shows this. It comes from one agent's judgment when writing a record. No release instruction caused it, and the README did not either. It is also not a harness mechanism: the sandbox, non-interactive exec, auto-approval, the simulated home and the relay played no part, and the harness note says nothing about delivery order. Nothing shows that the release causes it, so it cannot be called product. A defensible product reading is narrower: the README and skills never state the order, so an agent can invent a pre-release assembly step. A single occurrence that the user resolved correctly from the README does not establish that.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-status/scripts/collect_status.py:228 passes state.md "Next steps" through unchanged. awb-status/SKILL.md:60 suggests "Mark the <package> package delivered" with no assembly step first. awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:32 leaves the footer's next step to the agent. awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:2590 has START-HERE say "the deck, once you build it". awb-package/assets/package-format/deck-rules.md:87 sends content changes back for a refreshed package. README.md:9-28 is silent on order but does not put building first. The step itself was written by the agent: co2-A/relay/agent-005.jsonl `state next --add "...then assemble and visually check the PowerPoint using START-HERE.md..."`.

verdicts.reasoning:
The evidence IDs in the finding point to the wrong entries. co2-A-12 is about headline-preview.md and taxi-A-25 is about sandbox warnings. The entries that actually match are co2-A-10 and taxi-A-23.

taxi-A shows no problem. The user and agent both say START-HERE made it clear the package is an outline plus chart files, and the user accepted that (taxi-A/feedback/agent.md:37, 170). None of taxi-A's footers mention a build-or-release order. Saying the package is not a PPTX is a deliberate, documented design choice, not a defect.

Only co2-A shows the confusion about order, and the agent's own wording triggered it, not any release text. In reply 5 the agent added its own next-step entry with `state next --add "Review the corrected donor-roundtable working copy, then assemble and visually check the PowerPoint using START-HERE.md..."` (co2-A/relay/agent-005.jsonl, item_40). It then combined that entry with awb-status's "Mark the package delivered" request into its footer: "next: assemble and review PowerPoint, then 'Mark donor-roundtable delivered'". No release file says to assemble or review the PowerPoint before release. Searching the release for "assemble", "visual" and "before/after release" finds nothing of the kind.

The released design points the other way:
- The README says the end product is the package and "It is not a .pptx".
- START-HERE ships inside every release and lists "the deck, once you build it as part 2 says".
- The deck-rules revision boundary sends content changes back for a revised package and a rebuild.

The co2-A user read it the same way ("The README presents the package as the deliverable") and was only unsure because of the agent's footer. They released, and that "was fine". The README is silent on the order, as the finding says, but that silence did not cause the confusion. Of the six runs, only co2-A shows it, and an agent improvising a next step caused it. The release text neither causes the problem nor contradicts the right order. At most a one-line README note would be optional polish.
verdicts.release_evidence: No release file tells anyone to build the deck before release. These say the package is the deliverable and the deck is built from it: README.md:9 ("It is not a .pptx. Nothing in the workbench draws slides."), README.md:22-27 (how to build from the files), README.md:31 and :104 (marking it delivered makes a frozen release of the package). awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:2593 writes START-HERE with "the deck, once you build it as part 2 says". awb-package/references/package-contract.md:21 says START-HERE serves "whoever holds the package or a release". awb-package/assets/package-format/deck-rules.md:87 says content changes need a revised package and a rebuild. awb-status/SKILL.md:60 offers "Mark the <package> package delivered" with no deck-building step before it. The PowerPoint-first wording came from the agent: co2-A/relay/agent-005.jsonl item_40 (state next --add "...then assemble and visually check the PowerPoint..."), then reported at co2-A/transcript.md:310 and :314.

consolidated.title: validate.py crashes with KeyError 'left_rows' when a joins check omits it
consolidated.description: A joins spec without left_rows raises a traceback for each result instead of returning a validation error. The settings template comment does not say left_rows is required.
consolidated.evidence: co2-B-12: traceback in agent-002; awb_validate.py:124; settings.toml:33 comment. retail-B-22: src/exploration/validate.py _joins.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and found none. The crash comes from release code that reached both projects unchanged.

1. **Same code in both projects.** The project copies of validate.py in co2-B and retail-B are byte-identical to the release's awb-init/assets/awb_validate.py. Both investigations' run.py files are byte-identical to the release template. So the simulated home folder did not alter any of it, and neither did the skill copy or the relay.

2. **The defect.** `_joins` (awb_validate.py:124) reads `join["left_rows"]` with no check for the key. A joins spec that omits it raises a bare KeyError, not a validation message. That contrasts with `validate()` itself, which raises clear ValueErrors for an unknown spec key and for an invalid judgment.

3. **Why "a traceback for each result".** run.py:166-170 catches each result's exception, calls traceback.print_exc() and prints `{"error": "KeyError: 'left_rows'"}`, then moves to the next result.

4. **The documented pattern leads here.** run.py `_spec` (lines 97-102) merges a producer's measured dict into the static joins dict. The settings.toml:33 comment says "left_rows usually from a producer", and validation.md:11 describes producers supplying `joins.left_rows`. Read together, these present a settings-side `joins = { keys, keys_unique }` with left_rows filled in at run time as the intended use. But the default producer returns `{}`, and a custom producer may return only row_counts. In either case the merged spec has no left_rows and the run crashes. Nothing in the template or validation.md says left_rows must be set in settings when no producer supplies it.

5. **Evidence from the runs.**
   - co2-B: relay/agent-002.jsonl shows settings with `joins = { keys = ["country"], keys_unique = true }` and no producer. The run printed a KeyError traceback at validate.py:124 for 6 of 7 results. The agent then added static `left_rows = 20/45/4/59` to fix it.
   - retail-B: relay/agent-002.jsonl shows the same traceback for product-cancellation and country-growth. Their producers returned only row_counts. The agent fixed it by returning `"joins": {"left_rows": ...}` from those producers.

6. **Harness factors ruled out.**
   - The agent in both B runs was Claude Code, not Codex, so the Codex sandbox played no part.
   - Running non-interactively changes nothing: run.py prints the traceback the same way in any terminal.
   - No MCP auto-approval, relay mistake or persona answer was involved. The spec was written by the agent following the release's own template and docs.
   - Two of six runs, on different datasets, independently wrote the same partial spec. That points to the docs inviting it, not to a quirk of one run.

A real user on a normal host, or their agent, writing joins without left_rows and without a producer that supplies it, would hit the same traceback. Severity minor is fair: run.py keeps going after each failure, and the one-line error names the missing key.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/awb_validate.py:124 (`keys, left_rows = join["keys"], join["left_rows"]`, no check that the key exists); awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/settings.toml:33 ("left_rows usually from a producer", never says it is required); awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/run.py:97-102 (`_spec` merges producer entries into static joins) and :166-170 (prints a traceback per result); awb-init/references/validation.md:11,15

verdicts.reasoning:
The shipped helper reads the key with no check. awb_validate.py line 124 is `keys, left_rows = join["keys"], join["left_rows"]`, and nothing earlier in validate() checks the shape of a joins spec. If a joins spec reaches it without left_rows, it raises a bare KeyError. The same helper does check judgment specs (_judgment raises a ValueError that explains what to supply), so the joins check falls short of the helper's own standard.

run.py's main() catches the exception, prints a full traceback and writes `{"result_id": ..., "error": "KeyError: 'left_rows'"}`, then goes on to the next result. So "crash" really means a traceback and a failed result for every affected result, not the whole process dying.

The docs do not prevent this. They arguably invite it:
- The settings.toml template comment (line 33) shows `joins = { keys = [...], left_rows = N, keys_unique = true }  # left_rows usually from a producer` and never says the key is required.
- validation.md line 11 says producers extend the spec with `joins.left_rows`.
- validation.md line 15 gives a default only for keys_unique.

A user could reasonably write keys plus keys_unique in settings and expect left_rows to be optional or filled in later.

The run evidence confirms it happened:
- co2-B: in relay/agent-002.jsonl, line 181 adds `joins = { keys = ["country"], keys_unique = true }` to settings. Line 182's tool result shows the traceback through validate.py:124 _joins and five `"error": "KeyError: 'left_rows'"` lines. Line 197 fixes it by adding explicit left_rows values.
- retail-B: the agent read validation.md (agent-002.jsonl line 237) before writing settings (line 256). Line 274 shows the same KeyError traceback, and line 279 fixes it by having the producers return `"joins": {"left_rows": ...}`.

Neither run needed anything specific to the harness. Any user on a normal host would hit this, since it is plain helper code. Both agents recovered in one step, which fits the minor severity.
