Interactive Codex would most likely get the same model and the same base instructions, though I did not check the TUI's prompt; nothing in exec/resume, the sandbox or the simulated home changes link formatting. So "harness" does not fit. With release causation not shown and the "may not open" impact never tested, the finding is unsupported.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:28 ("Answer in chat, giving file paths"): neutral, and does not contradict the Codex host's base_instructions, which require absolute link targets. awb-package/SKILL.md:91 ("the draft path") plus check-draft returning a project-relative `draft` field could prime relative links, but retail-A/relay/agent-005.jsonl got that output and used absolute links, and retail-A/relay/agent-001.jsonl and agent-004.jsonl used relative links without it. No release line causes the switch.

verdicts.reasoning:
The switch is real, but the release does not cause it, and nothing shows a link failing to open.

What the transcripts show: in taxi-A, file links use absolute targets in replies 1-5 (transcript lines 47-225). Replies 6 and 7 use project-relative links such as `[Full slide draft](deliveries/.../draft/findings.md)` (lines 260-262 and 334). Reply 8 goes back to absolute links (line 366). In co2-A, only reply 4 (lines 263-265) uses relative links; replies 1-3, 5 and 6 are absolute.

The finding cites the wrong IDs. The original entries are taxi-A-29 and co2-A-13, not taxi-A-31 and co2-A-17 (co2-A-17 is about storyline order). Both referees tagged them "unclear".

What the release says: the project instructions only say "Answer in chat, giving file paths" (AGENTS.md:28). They never ask for relative links, and no template or README text shows relative chat links.

What the host says: the Codex CLI used (codex-cli 0.159.3) carries its own explicit rule in its base instructions. Clickable file links should look like `[app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12)`, with a "plain label, absolute target". So the host already prevents this. The agent followed that rule in most replies and broke it in 3 of 14 replies across the two cited runs.

One release-side contributor exists, and it is weak. check-draft returns a project-relative `draft` path (`awb_draft.py:2638`, built with `_rel()` at lines 70-74), and awb-package/SKILL.md:91 says to report "the draft path". The drifting turns (taxi-A 6 and 7, co2-A 4) all saw that output. But the same output came before absolute links in taxi-A reply 8 and co2-A reply 5. retail-A also mixes styles, and its relative links point at `../agent-home/.agents/skills/...` paths in the init and status turns, which no helper emits. Its full-draft handoff stayed absolute. This looks like intermittent drift by the Codex model away from its host's own rule, not something a release instruction produces.

The harm is also unproven. Neither simulated user failed to open a file: one noted a "minor inconsistency", the other "fine in an IDE, awkward in a terminal". The Claude-agent runs (B) used project-relative code spans consistently, so the switching itself shows up only on Codex.
verdicts.release_evidence: The release has no instruction that causes the switch. AGENTS.md:28 ("Answer in chat, giving file paths; never say a file was attached or sent.") says nothing about path form. A minor contributor: awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:2638 (check-draft returns `"draft": _rel(root, draft)`, project-relative) plus awb-package/SKILL.md:91 ("Report ... the draft path"). The host contradicts the finding: Codex base instructions say clickable links use an "absolute target", and the agent followed that in 11 of 14 replies.

consolidated.title: Methods note length is not checked against the length the user asked for
consolidated.description: #61's audience-facing methods note is short in most runs (taxi-A's is about 400 words). Its template allows 'a page or two' with no word budget, and nothing checks the length stated in the brief. taxi-B's first note ran far past one page while the report called it a one-page note. Length was enforced only after the agent added R-methodology-note-001, and the released note has 506 words.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-09: methodology-note-template.md 'Keep it to a page or two'; the brief says 'one-page methodology note'; msg 6 'Reduce it to about 500 words'.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to pin this on the harness and couldn't.

What happened: in message 1 the user asked for "about 8 slides ... plus a one-page methodology note". The agent wrote that length into the brief's Audience section ("Deck length: about 8 slides plus a one-page methodology note"). Its first methodology-note.md was 770 words (agent-005.jsonl line 208, Write). Fixes made during the review loop added text, and I counted the words in each snapshot under agent-home/scratch: review-1 has 770, review-15 has 867. Reply 5 then told the user the draft was "a one-page methodology note" and that the reviews were clean (transcript lines 409 and 414).

In message 6 the user said the note was too long for one page and asked for about 500 words. The agent added R-methodology-note-001 (warning, document scope, "about 500 words"). Snapshots review-16 and review-17 hold 530 and 534 words. At release the review flagged 541 words against the new rule, and the released note is 506 words (storage/releases/.../001/methodology-note.md).

The release has no check that would catch this:
- methodology-note-template.md line 7 allows "Keep it to a page or two". That is looser than the one-page note the README's own example asks for (README.md:46).
- awb-package/SKILL.md:28 records a stated length in Audience. SKILL.md:52 and :91 report main and appendix slide counts against that length, but the methods note has no matching step.
- check-draft (awb_draft.py) caps headlines at 15 words (HEADLINE_WORDS) and does not measure the note's length at all.
- references/review.md does not check the note's length against the brief.

Harness explanations I checked and rejected:
- Persona front-loading: "one-page" is the phrasing the README's example prompt suggests, and stating it early only made the length known sooner.
- Non-interactive `claude -p`, sandbox, simulated home, auto-approved tools: none of these affects whether anything compares the note to the recorded length. The reviews ran as subagents inside one turn, as they would on an interactive host.
- Relay: the false "one-page" claim is in the agent's own reply, passed on verbatim.
- Codex user being strict: 867 words of Markdown with seven sections is plausibly two pages, so a real user who asked for one page would notice. The user's notes say "far too long in ordinary formatting".

Caveats:
- It reproduced in only one of the two runs that stated a length. taxi-A's Codex agent wrote 399 words. Other runs wrote 635 to 884 words, but their users asked only for a "methodology note" or a "short" one, with no page length. So whether the gap shows depends on the agent model. Claude Code is a host the release targets, so this is still the release's gap.
- The finding cites "taxi-B-09" for its evidence, but in findings.json taxi-B-09 is the payment-code re-ask. The note-length issue is recorded as taxi-B-02 and taxi-B-28.
- "Far past one page" is a little strong: 867 words is about 1.7 times a 500-word page.

The finding's severity of minor fits.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/assets/package-format/methodology-note-template.md:7 ("Keep it to a page or two", no word budget, no reference to the recorded length); awb-package/SKILL.md:28, :52, :91 (length recorded in Audience but reported only as slide counts); awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:1772 (HEADLINE_WORDS = 15 is the only word limit, nothing for the note); awb-package/references/review.md:22 (no note-length check); README.md:46 (example asks for "a one-page methods note"). Run evidence: taxi-B/project/investigations/airport-trips-and-tipping/brief.md Audience; taxi-B/agent-home/scratch/review-1 to review-17 word counts; transcript.md lines 409, 414, 455; foundation/review-rules.md R-methodology-note-001

verdicts.reasoning:
The release has no way to hold the methods note to a length the user asks for, and its template permits a longer note.

Release side:
- methodology-note-template.md:7 says only "Keep it to a page or two", with no word budget.
- The brief template (brief.md:19) records a length only for the deck, "about 8 slides".
- awb-package/SKILL.md:28, :52 and :91 report main and appendix slide counts against the recorded length. Nothing reports or checks the note's length.
- The reviewer brief (references/review.md:15-25) never reads the brief's Audience section. Its step 3 checks support, caveats and claims, not length.
- check-draft (helpers.md:15) reads the note only for its names, Markdown, claims and numbers checks.
- The README's own example prompt (README.md:46) asks for "a one-page methods note", so the release expects this request and gives the user nothing that enforces it.

Run evidence in taxi-B confirms the finding:
- User message 1 asks for "a one-page methodology note". The agent recorded "about 8 slides plus a one-page methodology note" in investigations/airport-trips-and-tipping/brief.md (Audience).
- The first Write of the note in relay/agent-005.jsonl was 770 words.
- Over 13 review rounds it grew to 867 words (agent-home/scratch/review-1 to review-15 copies: 770, 780, ..., 867). That fits within "a page or two", and no check stopped it.
- The agent's report still called it "a one-page methodology note" (transcript line 409) and "the one-page note for the board" (line 414).
- The user (msg 6, line 455) replied "too long for one page. Reduce it to about 500 words".
- The agent then added R-methodology-note-001 (foundation/review-rules.md:32, warning, document scope). The note dropped to about 530 words (review-16).
- At release the rule flagged 541 words (line 550) and the agent trimmed. The released note is 506 words (storage/releases/.../001/methodology-note.md).

Corrections to the finding:
- "Short in most runs" is wrong. Only taxi-A's note is short (399 words). The other drafts run 635 to 884 words (co2-A 827, co2-B 884, retail-A 635, retail-B 838). This makes the finding stronger, not weaker.
- "Far past one page" is a slight overstatement: 867 words is about 1.7 pages.

The agent ignored a length the user stated and the brief recorded, which contributed. But no release instruction told it to honour that length, and the template's "a page or two" pointed it toward a longer note. A real user making the README's own one-page request would hit this. It is not a harness artefact: the simulated user noticed through normal review.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/assets/package-format/methodology-note-template.md:7 ("Keep it to a page or two", no word budget); awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/brief.md:19 (records only deck length); awb-package/SKILL.md:28,52,91 (only slide counts reported against recorded length); awb-package/references/review.md:22 (reviewer step 3 has no length check); README.md:46 (example prompt asks for "a one-page methods note")

consolidated.title: awb-status reports no open caveats while finding caveats remain
consolidated.description: Status said 'none open... the one recorded caveat is the kept repeated lines'. It left out the missing customer IDs, the first-observed definition, how cancellations are booked and the December 2011 exclusion, because the collector reports the issues in state.md, not the caveats on findings. #64 fixed the release report's caveat list (10.5), but awb-status has nothing equivalent.
consolidated.evidence: retail-B-11: A3 'Where we are'; U4 'The status summary understates the caveats'; awb-status 'Open work'.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not tie this to the harness. The cause is in the release's awb-status skill.

What happened in A3 (relay/agent-003.jsonl, entries 31 to 35): the agent loaded the awb-status skill, which is byte-identical to the release copy (diff -r found no differences), and called MCP `read status`. The collector's output included a `reason` for all eight findings. These were the caveats on each finding:
- Lines without a customer ID cannot be assigned, and 14.5% of revenue has no ID.
- "First purchase means first observed in this export", so early cohorts are biased.
- Cancellations count in the month booked and are not linked to the original sale.

The skill says to report only "every flagged finding in `active.findings` with its `reason`". All eight findings were provisional and none was flagged, so every one of those caveats was dropped. Under "Open work" the skill says to report `unresolved_issues`, and state.md listed only one there: the kept repeated lines (DQ-013, about £55k). The agent followed the skill and wrote "Open questions and caveats: none open. The one recorded caveat is the kept repeated lines and their £55k sensitivity." The relay passed that text to the persona unchanged (relay/human-004.in.md lines 77 to 79), and the persona raised it as pain point 7 in feedback/human.md.

Harness explanations I checked and ruled out:
- **Non-interactive claude -p:** the collector and the skill text behave the same in an interactive session.
- **Auto-approved MCP:** the status call succeeded, and approving it by hand would not change what it returns.
- **Codex sandbox:** it only applies to the human role.
- **Simulated home folder:** the installed skill is identical to the release.
- **Relay:** it carried the text faithfully.
- **Persona front-loading:** the question "Use awb-status — where are we" is an ordinary status request, and nothing in it steered the agent away from the caveats.

The fixed path has no equivalent here. awb-release/SKILL.md line 57 lists every `open_caveats` entry and forbids saying nothing is outstanding while one remains. awb-status has no such rule.

Two caveats on the finding itself:
1. The phrase "the one recorded caveat" is the model's own wording, and so is its choice not to put the no-ID coverage gap into `unresolved_issues` (the state.md template asks for coverage limitations there). Both would happen just the same for a real user on an interactive host, so they do not make this a harness artifact.
2. The December 2011 exclusion was not yet in the finding caveats at A3. It was added later, as the final state.md shows. That one item in C-71 is overstated; the other three omitted caveats were recorded at A3.

Severity minor stands.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-status/SKILL.md:27 says to report only "every flagged finding in `active.findings` with its `reason`", and awb-status/SKILL.md:28 says to report `unresolved_issues` as Open work. awb-status/scripts/collect_status.py:211 and :223 read the "Revalidation reason or caveat" column of state.md for every finding, so the caveats were in the output but the skill drops them for findings that are not flagged. For comparison, awb-release/SKILL.md:57 lists every open_caveats entry and awb-status has no equivalent rule.

verdicts.reasoning:
I checked the cited evidence and it shows the problem. In retail-B, the agent ran awb-status in turn 3 (relay/agent-003.jsonl, event 35). The collector's output listed the caveat on each of the eight provisional findings in active.findings[].reason. Those caveats included the lines without a customer ID, the first-observed-in-this-export definition, and cancellations counted in the month booked. The collector's unresolved_issues held a single item: the kept repeated lines. The agent then reported "Open questions and caveats: none open. The one recorded caveat is the kept repeated lines and their £55k sensitivity" (transcript.md:247). The simulated user objected straight away: "The status summary understates the caveats" (transcript.md, user message 4). The same complaint appears in feedback/human.md:17.

The release causes this. awb-status/SKILL.md:27 tells the agent to report the caveat ("reason") only for flagged findings. SKILL.md:28 limits "Open work" to unresolved_issues and next_steps. With no flagged findings, the caveats on supported or provisional findings are filtered out by instruction. Nothing in the skill stops the agent from saying there are no caveats. awb-release has that guard (awb-release/SKILL.md:57: list every open_caveats entry and never say nothing is outstanding while one remains; CHANGELOG.md:47). awb-status has no equivalent, as the finding says. A real user running "where are we?" after findings carry caveats would get the same incomplete picture.

Three qualifiers:
1. The finding gets one mechanism wrong. The collector does return the caveats on findings. SKILL.md drops them, not the collector.
2. The agent shares some blame. Its own collector data contradicted "the one recorded caveat". Also, awb-explore/SKILL.md:46 asks for shared coverage limitations, such as missing customer IDs, to be recorded under Unresolved issues, which the agent did not do.
3. At turn 3, the December 2011 exclusion was recorded in no finding caveat or issue, so status could not have reported it. That part of the finding is not supported.

Overall it is a product issue of minor severity.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-status/SKILL.md:27 (the Findings item reports the reason only for "every flagged finding"); awb-status/SKILL.md:28 (Open work is limited to unresolved_issues and next_steps); collect_status.py:223-228 (returns the caveat of every finding as "reason", so the data was available); no guard against claiming there are no caveats, unlike awb-release/SKILL.md:57 and CHANGELOG.md:47. Run evidence: retail-B/transcript.md:247; retail-B/relay/agent-003.jsonl event 35; retail-B/feedback/human.md:17

consolidated.title: README lists clean and explore as usual steps, but agents fold them into other steps
consolidated.description: The README's ordered list of requests (#67) presents clean and explore as steps 3 and 4. The agent folded both into landing and analysis without saying so, and the user was left unsure whether something had been skipped. The conditional wording ('It helps when...') is easy to miss.
consolidated.evidence: retail-A-08: A2; README 'The usual requests, in order', items 3-4; human notes turn 3.

verdicts.reasoning:
The behaviour happened as described. In reply 2 the user had asked only to "bring the data in once scope is settled", yet the Codex agent landed the data, ran its checks as ad hoc exploration queries, ran all five analyses and wrote the headline preview. It never invoked awb-clean or awb-explore and never said it was skipping them. At turn 3 the user wrote "It never ran a separate clean or explore step, which the README lists as steps 3 and 4. Unclear whether that matters" (human/notes.md), and repeated the point in feedback/human.md item 6.

Harness causes I checked and ruled out:
- **Relay:** messages pass verbatim and the interim messages were relayed.
- **Codex sandbox and auto-approved MCP:** nothing in the turn depended on them.
- **Non-interactive exec pressure:** the rollout's developer text is Codex's ordinary Default collaboration mode ("strongly prefer making reasonable assumptions and executing"), which is also the interactive default. The approval_policy=never text only forbids sandbox escalation. There is no exec-only "finish before yielding" instruction.
- **Front-loading:** the user's rich first message follows the README's own advice ("The more you put in the first message, the fewer questions follow"), and front-loaded facts do not explain why the clean step was skipped.
- **Agent choice:** agent-notes.md says the agent read awb-clean/SKILL.md and chose to bypass it, because the skill would ask the user to choose which rows win even for the proven duplicate overlap (finding retail-A-08, a product finding).

One harness confound remains. The shared persona brief (kit/human-rules.md:31, "The path to the end point") explicitly lists "get the data in → check/clean it → explore it", which primes the simulated user to expect those steps. It does not explain the finding, for two reasons:
- The user cited the README, not the brief, and the README the user received is byte-identical to the release README. Its "The usual requests, in order" (README.md:75-88) numbers Clean and Explore as steps 3 and 4. The only signals that they are optional are the conditional "It helps…" sentences and line 88's "awb-status suggests clean and explore when they fit". A real user reading only the README gets the same expectation.
- Nothing in the release tells the agent to offer or mention clean/explore after landing. awb-clean/SKILL.md:3 and awb-explore/SKILL.md:3 trigger only on request, and awb-scope/SKILL.md:63 routes data questions "for awb-explore or analysis". So the silent folding follows the release as written.

Why confidence is medium rather than high:
- It comes from one run. co2-A had the same setup and the same folding (its user noted "one long turn did scope + landing + all analysis + headline preview") and did not flag it.
- The user called it mild confusion ("That turned out fine").
- The brief adds to the priming.

The mismatch between the README's ordered list and how agents actually behave is still a release issue that a real interactive user could hit.
verdicts.release_evidence: README.md:75-88 ("The usual requests, in order" numbers 3. Clean and 4. Explore as steps; the only optional signals are the conditional "It helps…" sentences and line 88's "awb-status suggests clean and explore when they fit"). awb-clean/SKILL.md:3 and awb-explore/SKILL.md:3 trigger only on request, and awb-scope/SKILL.md:63 routes data questions to "awb-explore or analysis", so no agent instruction says to offer or mention clean/explore after landing. Run evidence: retail-A/transcript.md reply 2; retail-A/human/notes.md Turn 3; retail-A/feedback/agent-notes.md lines 21 and 25 (awb-clean read and deliberately bypassed). Harness confound, not causal: kit/human-rules.md:31 (the brief's path lists check/clean and explore).

verdicts.reasoning:
The run evidence holds up. In A1 (relay/agent-001.out.md:34) the agent laid out its plan as download, analyze, then headline preview, with no clean or explore step. In A2 (relay/agent-002.out.md) it landed the data, handled the 1-9 Dec 2010 sheet overlap inside the investigation rather than through awb-clean, ran the exploration SQL inline and reported '5 answered'. It described those data checks in plain words, but it never said that no cleaning or exploration pass had run, or why. The user's notes for Turn 3 (human/notes.md) say: 'It never ran a separate clean or explore step, which the README lists as steps 3 and 4. Unclear whether that matters.' feedback/human.md pain point 6 and its README section ('Missing: that the clean and explore steps are optional, or folded into the analysis') say the same. The referee recorded it too (orchestrator-report.md pain point 8, A2).

The release causes it:
- **README framing.** The README puts Clean and Explore as items 3 and 4 under the heading 'The usual requests, in order'. The only sign that they are optional is a trailing 'It helps when...' sentence at the end of each item. Line 88 says only that awb-status suggests them, and status did not run until after the answers.
- **The README's own condition was met.** Item 3 says cleaning 'helps before you analyze a dataset nobody has checked', and this dataset had not been checked. So the README itself suggests the step applied here.
- **No skill tells the agent to explain.** Nothing in the project AGENTS.md, awb-init or awb-scope tells the agent to say when cleaning or exploration is folded into landing or analysis. AGENTS.md lets preparation stay bounded by the question, so skipping the passes breaks no instruction.
- **awb-clean pushes the agent away.** awb-clean/SKILL.md:31 makes 'whether repeated rows or keys are errors and which row wins' a decision the user must make. The agent's notes (feedback/agent-notes.md:25, feedback/agent.md item 5) cite this as the reason it skipped the cleaning pass, even though the overlap was proven exact.

A real user reading the same README on a normal host could hit the same uncertainty.

There are three caveats, which is why confidence is medium rather than high:
- **Harness priming.** human/BRIEF.md:68 tells the simulated user that a successful session includes 'check/clean it -> explore it'. That is harness priming a real user would not have, though the user's notes blame the README, which does list the steps.
- **The user never asked.** In taxi-B, co2-B and retail-B the users explicitly requested clean or explore. This user only said 'bring the data in'.
- **No cost.** The user never raised the doubt in chat, so it cost no exchanges. Minor severity fits.
verdicts.release_evidence: README.md:75 (heading 'The usual requests, in order'), README.md:81-82 (Clean and Explore as items 3-4, each made conditional only by a trailing 'It helps...' sentence; item 3 applies to 'a dataset nobody has checked'), README.md:88 (only awb-status is said to suggest them). awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md (Conversation and Analytical invariants sections) has no instruction to tell the user when cleaning or exploration is folded or skipped. awb-clean/SKILL.md:31 makes the user decide on repeated rows, which the agent cited as its reason for skipping the cleaning pass.

consolidated.title: datasets.toml template shows only inline tables, and long declarations fail to parse
consolidated.description: A long multi-line inline types table failed publish with a TOML parse error. The template shows only the one-line 'types = { ... }' form, not the subtable form a long declaration needs. Oct 15 taxi-B hit the identical error.
consolidated.oct15_ref: Oct 15 per-run taxi-B agent.md (same datasets.toml parse error); not in fix-plan
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-30: agent-002 'Invalid initial character for a key part (at line 9, column 104)'; template line 36.

verdicts.reasoning:
I couldn't find a harness cause. In taxi-B the agent was Claude (claude-opus-5-5 through claude -p; Codex played the human). In relay agent-002 it wrote foundation/datasets.toml with a `types = { ... }` inline table spread over three lines. `awb.py publish` then refused it with "Invalid initial character for a key part (at line 9, column 104)". The agent rewrote the table as a `[datasets.yellow_trips.checks.types]` subtable and publish went through.

None of the harness factors touch this step:
- The non-interactive run, the Codex sandbox (which applies to the human role, not the agent), auto-approved MCP tools, the simulated home folder, relaying and the persona don't change which TOML the agent writes or how the helper parses it.
- The parser is the release's: awb_landing.py `declared_checks()` (lines 323-339) calls `tomllib.loads`. tomllib implements TOML 1.0, which forbids newlines inside inline tables. The project venv is Python 3.13.5, and the release requires 3.11 or later (or tomli). I confirmed that this interpreter rejects a two-line inline table with the same error, so any normal host running a supported Python behaves the same way.
- A real user's agent could write the same multi-line table.

What the release contributes:
- The template at awb-init/assets/workbench/foundation/datasets.toml shows only one-line inline tables (key reference line 15, example line 36).
- Neither that file nor workbench-guides/data.md mentions the subtable form, or that an inline table must stay on one line.
- The parse error goes to the user as raw tomllib text.

The finding overstates two things:
- "Long declarations fail to parse" is wrong. Long declarations on one line parse fine: taxi-A line 11 and retail-A line 3 are very long one-line `types` tables, and all five other runs published without a TOML error. The parser test above also accepted a 15-key one-line table. Only an inline table broken across lines fails.
- It happened in 1 of 6 runs, and recovery took one edit with no user involvement. I did not find the Oct 15 taxi-B run, so I could not check the claimed repeat.

Severity minor stands. It's a release documentation gap: the template shows no multi-line form, and the parser rejects the one an agent tends to write for a long table. It should be reworded as "multi-line inline tables fail; the template doesn't show the subtable form", not "long declarations fail".
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/foundation/datasets.toml:15 and :36 (only the one-line `types = { ... }` form is shown, no subtable form); awb-init/assets/awb_landing.py:333-339 (tomllib.loads, TOML 1.0, error passed through as "foundation/datasets.toml: <tomllib message>"); counter-evidence to "long" wording: taxi-A/project/foundation/datasets.toml:11 and retail-A/project/foundation/datasets.toml:3 (long one-line tables that parsed)

verdicts.reasoning:
The run evidence holds up. In taxi-B, relay/agent-002.jsonl line 60 shows the agent writing foundation/datasets.toml with a `types = { ... }` inline table spread over three lines. Line 63 shows both publish calls failing with "ValueError: foundation/datasets.toml: Invalid initial character for a key part (at line 9, column 104)". Column 104 is the line break right after the trailing comma. I reproduced the error with Python's tomllib on a minimal two-line inline table. TOML 1.0 forbids line breaks inside inline tables but allows them inside arrays, and the same file's multi-line `columns` and `not_null` arrays parsed fine. That mismatch is the trap.

The release has nothing that prevents this:
- The template uses inline tables for every key whose value is a table: types, accepted_values, range and row_count.
- It never says an inline table must stay on one line.
- It never shows the `[datasets.<name>.checks.types]` subtable form, which the loader accepts. The agent's fix used that form and publish then passed with 25 checks.
- workbench-guides/data.md line 33 points agents at this template as the reference for the keys.
- declared_checks() in awb_landing.py only adds the file name to tomllib's raw message, so nothing tells the agent the cause is a line break inside an inline table.

The failure recurs across runs. dry3-co2-B has an identical template and hit the same error (feedback/agent.md item 9: "line 32, column 109"). Among the main runs, taxi-A and retail-A avoided it only by writing 252-character single-line types tables. co2-B wrapped its arrays but kept its inline tables on one line. Agents that wrap long lines at about 100 characters, as the template's own comments do, fall into this. It is not a harness artifact: the same template, parser and error would face a real user on an interactive host.

Why medium confidence rather than high: the immediate cause is the agent writing invalid TOML. The release contributes only by omission: one example style, and no one-line warning or subtable example. Recovery took a single tool call because the error gives the line and column. Severity minor is right.

I could not confirm the finding's "Oct 15 taxi-B" claim from these folders. The dry3-co2-B run, created 2026-10-16, is the second case I could verify.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/foundation/datasets.toml:15 (`types = { column = "DuckDB type" }`) and :36-41 (every table-valued key is shown only as a one-line inline table; no subtable form, no note that inline tables cannot span lines); awb-init/assets/awb_landing.py:335-338 (passes tomllib's raw "Invalid initial character for a key part" message through with only the file name added); awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md:33 (sends agents to this template as the documentation of the keys)

consolidated.title: awb-status upstream probe cannot check sources served without ETag or Last-Modified
consolidated.description: The UCI server sends neither header, so the upstream-change probe can never check this source. Oct 15 retail-B reported the same (probeable_files: 0).
consolidated.oct15_ref: Oct 15 per-run retail-B agent.md; not in fix-plan
consolidated.evidence: retail-B-33: land --request note 'server sent no ETag or Last-Modified'; the awb-status probe requires one of the two.

verdicts.reasoning:
I found nothing in the harness that caused this. The missing headers come from the UCI server, and the release's probe is built to depend on them.

1) The server really sends no validators. In the retail-B agent transcript (relay/agent-002.jsonl), the saved headers.txt shows only `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, `Server: nginx/1.31.4`, `Date`, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and `Connection`. Because the server name is nginx, the headers came from the origin and not from a proxy. I sent my own HEAD request to the same URL from outside the sim sandbox and got the same result: no ETag, no Last-Modified and no Content-Length. Any real user on any host gets this response.

2) The release is designed so this source can never be checked:
- awb-status/SKILL.md:18 limits `--probe-upstream` to HEAD requests, and only for files whose provenance records "an HTTP URL with an ETag or Last-Modified".
- collect_status.py:573-574 marks every other file not probeable, with the reason "no ETag or Last-Modified recorded".
- awb-init/references/landing.md:11 makes the same requirement.
- There is no other way to check: no fallback that downloads the file and hashes it, and no comparison of Content-Length.

The awb-status run in agent-003.jsonl reported `"upstream":{"probeable_files":0}`, which matches the finding.

3) I ruled out each harness explanation:
- **Codex sandbox:** the agent in this run was Claude, not Codex (Codex played the human).
- **Personas:** the human never asked about upstream changes. The agent noticed the problem on its own while landing the data (feedback/agent.md §3).
- **Relay mistakes, auto-approved tools, simulated home:** none of these affects which HTTP headers a public server returns.

Caveats:
- The finding's evidence ID is wrong. In retail-B/feedback/findings.json, retail-B-33 is a different finding, about scratch files written to /tmp. The real evidence is feedback/agent.md §3, provenance.json and foundation/sources.md, whose request field says "server sent no ETag or Last-Modified".
- The agent recorded `upstream: null` rather than a bare URL. The file is therefore counted under without_upstream instead of listed as not_probeable. Either way the probe cannot check it.
- The release does report this honestly rather than giving a wrong result. So this is a documented design limitation that real users will run into on validator-less servers like UCI, not a bug in how the code behaves. Minor severity is about right.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-status/scripts/collect_status.py:573-574 (a file without a recorded etag or last_modified goes to not_probeable with the reason "no ETag or Last-Modified recorded"); awb-status/SKILL.md:18 (the probe sends HEAD requests only, and only for files with an HTTP URL plus an ETag or Last-Modified); awb-init/references/landing.md:11 (the same requirement)

verdicts.reasoning:
The behaviour is real, and the release's design is the reason it happens. It is a documented limit, not a bug.

Run evidence (retail-B):
- inbox/uci-download-2026-10-16/headers.txt holds the headers of the agent's real curl GET to archive.ics.uci.edu (relay/agent-002.jsonl). They are 200 OK, Server nginx/1.31.4, Date, Transfer-Encoding: chunked and Connection, with no ETag or Last-Modified.
- I sent a read-only HEAD to the same URL today and got the same result: no ETag and no Last-Modified. A real user on a normal host would hit this too.
- The request field in project/data/raw/online-retail-ii/2026-10-16-uci/provenance.json says 'server sent no ETag or Last-Modified', and both files record upstream: null.
- The collect_status output in relay/agent-003.jsonl shows "upstream":{"probeable_files":0}.

Release cause:
- collect_status.py puts any file without an etag or last_modified string under not_probeable, with the reason "no ETag or Last-Modified recorded".
- awb-status/SKILL.md:18 limits the probe to files whose provenance records an HTTP URL with an ETag or Last-Modified.
- landing.md:11 says the probe works only with those validators.
- There is no fallback, such as Content-Length, or a GET compared against the SHA-256 that provenance already records. So any source served without validators can never be checked, as the finding says.

The release handles this gracefully: it reports such files as 'not checked' with a reason and does not fail. That makes this a minor capability gap, not a defect. In this run probeable_files was 0 for a second reason too: the agent landed with the `land` CLI and recorded no upstream URL at all. But even with a URL recorded, the file would have been not_probeable for lack of validators, so the finding holds either way.

Corrections to the finding:
- The cited evidence ID 'retail-B-33' is wrong. In feedback/findings.json, retail-B-33 is about scratch files written to /tmp. The matching entry is retail-B-26 (findings.json:293, feedback/agent.md:49).
- I could not check the 'Oct 15 retail-B' claim from these run folders.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-status/scripts/collect_status.py:573-574 (not_probeable, reason "no ETag or Last-Modified recorded"); awb-status/SKILL.md:18 (the probe sends HEAD only for files with an HTTP URL plus an ETag or Last-Modified); awb-init/references/landing.md:11

consolidated.title: Settings 'views' key accepts logical names unvalidated, and staleness checks later fail
consolidated.description: The settings 'views' key accepted logical view names. Results ran and passed their runtime checks, but stale later reported missing evidence and looked for a nonexistent path. run.py reads config.get('views') without validation, and the settings template does not document the key.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-15: run.py template line 122; final settings.toml lines 49 onward use paths.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not tie this to the harness. Every part of the failure comes from the release's own code and documentation.

What happened (relay/agent-002.jsonl):
- Item 44: the Codex agent wrote `views = ["yellow_trips", "taxi_zones"]` into each new results table, directly under `inputs = ["yellow_trips", "taxi_zones"]`.
- Item 45: `mcp__awb__run` finished every result with `failed_checks: []`.
- Item 48: `read stale` then marked all 4 results stale with "missing evidence: yellow_trips: missing sha256" and an ENOENT on `<project>/yellow_trips`.
- Item 51: the agent rewrote the entries as `foundation/views/*.sql` paths. These are the paths at line 49 onward of the final settings.toml.

Why the release is the cause:
- run.py template line 123 passes `config.get("views")` straight to `record_evidence`. The only guidance is the comment on line 122, which never says the entries must be file paths.
- `result_problems` (awb_provenance.py:633-690) checks the question, inputs, code, parameters and answers, but never views.
- `file_checksums` (awb_provenance.py:78-98) records a missing file with null bytes and sha256 rather than raising. A bad entry therefore passes the run and only shows up at `stale`.
- The settings.toml template never mentions `views`. It does say `inputs` names "the datasets or views the producer reads", which makes the logical-name reading natural.
- references/provenance.md:13 says to set `views = [...]` without giving a format, and the agent never read that file.

Harness factors I checked and ruled out:
- Non-interactive codex exec: has no bearing on how a config key is interpreted.
- Auto-approved MCP `run`: an interactive user approving the call would see the same clean output, since the run reported no failure.
- Simulated home folder: skills loaded normally from ~/.agents/skills.
- Persona front-loading: the user's answers in that turn did not touch settings or views.
- Relay errors: none involved.

The trigger was the model choosing the optional override. The same model on a normal interactive host would read the same run.py comment and could make the same choice. The detection fallback would have worked without it.

Limits on impact:
- It happened in one run only. No other run's settings use `views`.
- The agent caught and fixed it within the same turn using `stale`, so no promoted finding was affected. Minor severity fits.

Note on the evidence citation: the finding's text matches taxi-A-14 in findings.json. taxi-A-15 is a different packaging-review finding, so the "taxi-A-15" in the evidence line is a mislabel. The content itself checks out.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/run.py:122-124 (views = config.get("views") or views_read(...), passed to record_evidence unvalidated); awb-init/assets/awb_provenance.py:633-690 (result_problems never checks views); awb-init/assets/awb_provenance.py:78-98 (file_checksums records missing files as null instead of raising); awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/settings.toml:12-41 (no views key documented; line 15 says inputs names datasets or views)

verdicts.reasoning:
The release causes this, and the run evidence shows it.

The shipped files:
- The run.py template (awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/run.py:122-123) reads the key with no checks: `views = config.get("views") or views_read(...)`. The only explanation is a comment saying the key overrides detection. It never says what form the entries take.
- The settings.toml template does not mention a `views` key at all. Its lines 14-15 describe `inputs` as naming "the datasets or views the producer reads". Those are logical names, so a reader is led to give `views` the same kind of value.
- awb-init/references/provenance.md:13 only says "Set `views = [...]` ... when its producer reads views its queries do not name". It does not say the entries must be project-relative view-definition file paths. The analysis guide also tells agents to read provenance.md only to adapt run.py's evidence recording, so it is off the normal path.
- Nothing rejects a bad entry. `result_problems()` (awb_provenance.py:633-683) checks the question, inputs, code, parameters and answers, but not views. `record_evidence()` passes the views to `file_checksums()`, which records a missing file as bytes/sha256 null instead of raising (awb_provenance.py:95-96). The run therefore succeeds and writes evidence that cannot be verified, and only `stale` notices later.

The run evidence (taxi-A):
- In relay/agent-002.jsonl the agent's settings write has `inputs = ["yellow_trips","taxi_zones"]` and `views = ["yellow_trips","taxi_zones"]` (line 88-89).
- The results ran and passed their checks. Then `awb read stale` reported 4 of 4 stale, with views failures "missing evidence: yellow_trips: missing sha256" and ENOENT for `<project>/yellow_trips` (line 97).
- The agent replaced the names with foundation/views/01_taxi_zones.sql and 02_yellow_trips.sql (line 101-102), and after that stale reported 0.
- The final project settings.toml lines 49 and 62 hold those paths, and the project's run.py matches the template around line 122.
- agent-notes.md and agent.md describe the same sequence.

The harness played no part. Any agent or user on a normal host who follows the settings template's wording would hit this.

Caveats:
- The agent may not have needed to set `views` at all, since detection might have found the views without it. That does not change the fact that the key's format is undocumented and unvalidated.
- `stale` caught the problem in the same turn, so no finding was affected. Minor severity fits.
- The evidence ID is mislabeled. This finding is taxi-A-14 in taxi-A/feedback/findings.json; taxi-A-15 there is a different finding about repeated package reviews.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/run.py:122-123 uses config.get("views") without validation. awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/settings.toml:14-15 describes `inputs` as names of datasets or views and never mentions a `views` key. awb-init/references/provenance.md:13 gives no format for `views`. awb-init/assets/awb_provenance.py:633-683 (`result_problems`) has no views check, and awb_provenance.py:95-96 (`file_checksums`) records missing paths as null instead of failing.

consolidated.title: No supported form for an access note when documentation cannot be retained
consolidated.description: The data guide expects a retained data dictionary, but offers no form for an access or assessment note when the original cannot be retained (the TLC PDF returned HTTP 403). It also has none for a code mapping that was not contemporaneous, such as Vendor 6.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-24: urllib HTTP 403 in agent-001; foundation/references/tlc-yellow/documentation-notes.md.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and found only partial ones. Neither explains the finding away.

(1) The persona front-loaded the condition. human/BRIEF.md:17 scripts "the site blocked the download". The user said exactly that in the opening message. That part is scenario setup. My own HEAD checks also suggest a real user's browser could save the PDF: the Python-urllib user agent gets 403, and a Chrome user agent gets 200.

(2) The agent's own fetch failure is not a sandbox artifact. relay/agent-001.jsonl line 41 shows urllib.error.HTTPError 403 Forbidden. That is a real HTTP response from nyc.gov, not a network-denied URLError. I reproduced the 403 from my host, outside the Codex sandbox, using the Python-urllib user agent. Any agent on a normal interactive host that fetches with urllib hits the same block.

(3) The Vendor 6 half has nothing to do with the harness or the retrieval. The only official dictionary available is the March 2025 revision. The data is from 2024. That gap would exist even with the PDF retained.

On the release side, the gap is real. workbench-guides/data.md:11 tells the agent to keep every dictionary an assessment relies on. It names two places: under foundation/references/, or at a retained location outside Git with a SHA-256. foundation/sources.md:16-21 accepts only two reference forms: a link to the copy, or a backticked location with sha256. It says "reference: not yet retained counts as no reference". awb-status/SKILL.md:32,48 then flags the source as a risk with "Keep the documentation". Nothing covers documentation that was consulted but cannot be retained, and nothing covers recording a document's revision against the period of the data. sources.md:23 says only to note failed acquisition attempts.

So the agent improvised. It wrote an analyst summary and linked it as the reference. The status check is syntax-only, so it counts that summary as a retained copy. A real user would hit this whenever documentation is blocked, behind a login, web-only, or a later revision than the data.

Impact was small. The agent coped, and the release package disclosed the gap. Minor severity is right. Confidence is medium rather than high because the scripted persona block did contribute to the trigger.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md:11 (dictionary must be kept: in references/ or outside Git with a SHA-256; no case for documentation that cannot be retained); awb-init/assets/workbench/foundation/sources.md:16-21 (only two reference forms; "reference: not yet retained counts as no reference"); sources.md:23 (only "Note failed acquisition attempts"); awb-status/SKILL.md:32,48 (flags the source as a risk: "Keep the documentation"). Nothing in the release covers a documentation revision that differs from the data period. Run evidence: taxi-A/relay/agent-001.jsonl line 41 (HTTP 403 from the server, not a sandbox block); taxi-A/human/BRIEF.md:17 (block scripted in the persona brief).

verdicts.reasoning:
The run evidence is real, but the cited ID is wrong. In taxi-A/feedback/findings.json the ID taxi-A-24 belongs to a README finding. This finding's text matches taxi-A-22, which comes from agent.md rank 11.

What the evidence shows:
- relay/agent-001.jsonl item_21 shows the agent calling urllib.request.urlopen on the TLC dictionary PDF. The call fails with "HTTP Error 403: Forbidden".
- The agent then read the PDF text through its web tool and wrote foundation/references/tlc-yellow/documentation-notes.md. That file is a self-described "analyst summary, not a copy of the dictionary", with the URL, the March 18, 2025 revision and the access date.
- The scenario itself sets up the case. The user's first message says they could not download the dictionary PDF because the site blocked it.
- nyc.gov rejecting a non-browser fetch is ordinary external behaviour, not a sandbox artifact. Documentation that is web-only or blocked from download is common, so a real user would meet this.

What the release says:
- workbench-guides/data.md line 11 requires keeping "each data dictionary, manual, codebook, or schema export that an assessment or catalog row relies on" under foundation/references/<source-id>/.
- Its only alternative is for material that licence or confidentiality keeps out of Git: store it outside the checkout and record its location and SHA-256. That still assumes you hold the file.
- foundation/sources.md lines 15-23 define exactly two reference forms: a link to the copy, or a retained location plus SHA-256. It says "reference: not yet retained" counts as no reference. Its "Note failed acquisition attempts" line is written for data acquisitions.
- awb-status (SKILL.md line 48; collect_status.py lines 404-406) would therefore list such a source as a standing risk ("Keep the documentation behind the <source> assessment"). Its only other outcome is to accept any link, including a summary written in place of the original.
- So nothing in the release describes an access or assessment note, or how to record a documentation revision that postdates the study period. The agent had to invent one, and the status check cannot tell that note apart from a retained original.

The impact is minor. The agent coped well, and the deliverable discloses the gap. The Vendor 6 part (a later revision used for a 2024 code) is weaker as a release defect, because it is mostly a domain judgment, though a revision/applicability field would cover it. The main gap, no supported form when the original cannot be retained, is real, and the release causes it.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md:11 (requires retaining each dictionary; only fallback is out-of-Git with a location and SHA-256); awb-init/assets/workbench/foundation/sources.md:15-23 (only two reference forms; "reference: not yet retained" counts as no reference; failed-attempt note covers acquisitions); awb-status/SKILL.md:32,48 and awb-status/scripts/collect_status.py:404-406 (a source assessed from documentation without a reference is flagged as a risk; any well-formed link, a summary included, passes)

consolidated.title: Question priority ties slide placement to decision gating
consolidated.description: In awb-scope, 'must' means the decision cannot be made without the answer, and findings-template puts every 'must' question on the Open questions slide. Making Vendor 6 'must' put it on that required slide even though it does not gate the airport decision, so the agent had to record the distinction itself.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-35: questions edit Q-009 --priority must in agent-006; awb-scope SKILL.md line 38; findings-template.md line 82.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and found none. The release forces this coupling.

1. **The user's request came up on its own.** In turn agent-005 the agent proposed a headline preview. It put only Q-011 (the code-99 zero tips) on the Open questions slide and kept Vendor 6 as a should-priority caveat (agent-notes.md line 71). The simulated user then asked: "Slide 8: it repeats slide 4. Make it the Open questions slide with both TLC questions (code-99 zeros and Vendor 6's identity)" (relay/agent-006.in.md). The persona brief (human/BRIEF.md) does not script this. It never mentions Vendor 6, the Open questions slide, or priorities. The user reached this from the agent's replies and the README, which describes Open questions as the place for unanswered questions the decision needs. A real first-time user on an interactive host could make the same request.

2. **The release leaves only one way to comply.** findings-template.md line 82 says to list "exactly the unanswered `must` ledger questions" on the slide. check-draft enforces this: awb_draft.py `open_question_problems` builds the expected bullets only from priority == "must" questions (lines 2489-2491). Any other bullet fails with "unexpected question or commentary" (lines 2536-2538). awb-scope SKILL.md line 38 defines `must` as "the decision cannot be made without its answer." So the only way to put Vendor 6 on the slide was to change the ledger priority. The agent did that: `questions edit Q-009 --priority must --audience ...` through the auto-approved awb MCP records tool, in agent-006.jsonl.

3. **The agent had to work around the mismatch itself.** Its history entry (history.md line 143) says the must priority "changes required slide membership, not an analytical assertion that funding must wait for that answer." feedback/agent.md line 33 asks the skill to separate slide membership from decision gating. The priority change has side effects beyond the slide. Q-009 is a root question (parent ""), so `must` changes its weight in finding order (findings-template line 13) and in status counts. It does not change any record's content.

4. **No harness factor explains it.** Non-interactive codex exec did not matter. Had the agent paused to ask, the options would be the same: decline the user's request, or mark a non-gating question `must`. The sandbox, the simulated home folder, the relay, and MCP auto-approval played no part. The command succeeded, and an interactive host would also have allowed it. No relay mistake appears either: the request reached the agent word for word.

**Counterpoint, which does not change the verdict:** the README frames Open questions as being for questions the decision needs. So one could say the release works as designed and the agent should have pushed back. Even so, the release gives no supported path for a user-requested question that does not gate the decision, and the only workaround misuses a field whose meaning other features depend on. A real user would hit this, and the release causes it. Severity minor, as filed.

The finding's evidence ID "taxi-A-35" does not appear in taxi-A/feedback/findings.json, which stops at taxi-A-29. I verified the claim against the primary sources instead: relay/agent-006.in.md, relay/agent-006.jsonl, history.md, questions.json, and feedback/agent.md.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/assets/package-format/findings-template.md:82 (list exactly the unanswered must questions), awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:2489-2491 and 2536-2538 (check-draft takes the required set only from must questions and rejects any other bullet), awb-scope/SKILL.md:38 (must = decision cannot be made without the answer)

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding holds, and the release causes it. In agent-006.in.md the user asked for slide 8 to become the Open questions slide with both TLC questions, tipping first. Until then Q-009 (Vendor 6) was `should` (agent-notes line 71 calls it "not an extra required question bullet"). The release ties slide membership to `must` and nothing else:
- findings-template.md line 82 says the slide lists "exactly the unanswered `must` ledger questions".
- package-contract.md line 37 says the same.
- awb_draft.py lines 2491-2492 select only priority=="must" questions, and lines 2539-2541 fail any other bullet as "unexpected question or commentary".

The only way to grant the user's request was therefore `questions edit Q-009 --priority must`. The agent ran exactly that in agent-006.jsonl (item_8, exit 0). But awb-scope SKILL.md line 38 defines `must` as "when the decision cannot be made without its answer", and Vendor 6 identity does not gate the airport decision. So the agent wrote the distinction down by hand, in three places:
- the brief: "Vendor 6 confirmation is context, not a demonstrated barrier to airport funding"
- the slide notes: "The board can discuss airport research ... without treating either context question as settled"
- agent-notes line 81: "required audience content, not an analytical funding gate"

The final questions.json shows Q-009 as must/open/root, and draft/findings.md lines 108-115 put it on the slide. The release handles finding order differently: a `presentation_order` override exists so that reordering slides leaves "ledger priority and parent unchanged" (awb-package SKILL.md line 52; package-contract.md line 35). Open questions membership has no such override, so priority does two jobs. A real user who wants a non-gating stakeholder question shown on that slide will hit this on any host. Minor severity: the agent coped by recording the caveat.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-scope/SKILL.md:38 (must = decision cannot be made without answer); awb-package/assets/package-format/findings-template.md:82 and awb-package/references/package-contract.md:37 (slide lists exactly the unanswered must questions; membership set only by ledger priority); awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:2491-2492 and 2539-2541 (check-draft fails any non-must bullet on the slide); no counterpart to the presentation_order override (awb-package/SKILL.md:52, package-contract.md:35) for Open questions membership

consolidated.title: awb-clean pushes confirmation of treatments that follow from the user's own principle
consolidated.description: The agent asked the user to confirm how to treat payment code 0, although the user had already set the principle and excluding code 0 from card tipping follows from it. awb-clean's rule that 'the user decides every other issue' drives this.
consolidated.oct15_ref: new; related to fix-plan section 3 (approval stops)
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-15: msg 2 states the principle; the reply 2 decision table marks Payment code 0 as 'Confirm'.

verdicts.reasoning:
The evidence doesn't show the simulation caused this, and it doesn't show the release caused it either.

What actually happened:
- In reply 1 the agent raised payment code 0 itself. In msg 2 the user replied: "Investigate payment code 0, but don't treat it alone as proof that a trip is invalid."
- In reply 2 the agent reported what it found. The TLC dictionary calls code 0 a "Flex Fare trip". These records are missing five fields. 22% of them show a tip, yet the payment method is not recorded.
- It then put a "Payment code 0 | Confirm" row in its decision table. The row proposed counting these trips everywhere except credit-card tipping and showing them separately. Its alternative was to also report their recorded tips as a separate figure.
- The user complained about this in human/notes.md turn 3 and feedback/human.md item 7 (finding taxi-B-09).

Why it is not a harness artifact:
- The persona brief (human/BRIEF.md) says nothing about payment code 0, so this is not front-loading. The user was reacting to the agent's own reply 1.
- The relay passed the messages unchanged.
- Codex sandboxing, MCP approval and the simulated home play no part.
- The agent's system note says to end the turn when it needs an answer. That is how an interactive host behaves too.
- One harness effect is real but small. The brief tells the persona to call out repeated questions, which makes it more likely to complain about a single re-confirmation.

Why the release is not shown to be the cause:
- Code 0 was never a scan issue. foundation/scans/yellow_trips.json holds S1-S13 (negatives, ranges, extremes, text-typed), and none of them is about payment_type. So awb-clean's "the user decides every other issue" did not push it into the table as an open scan decision.
- In the same turn the agent recorded that cleaning "awaits two user decisions": fares over $500 and negative charges on positive-fare trips. That is in relay/agent-002.jsonl, in the `state issues --add` call. The agent itself did not treat code 0 as an open awb-clean decision. The Confirm row was the model's own courtesy check on a treatment it had worked out.
- awb-clean never says to re-ask a decision the user has already given. Its line 29 says to record a user decision precisely so it "would otherwise be asked again" does not happen.

Why "redundant" overstates it:
- The user's principle was about validity. Leaving code 0 out of card tipping follows from Q3's "credit-card trips" scope, not from that principle.
- With tips on 22% of these trips and no payment method recorded, whether some of them are card trips was a real question.
- The row offered a real alternative (reporting their tips separately), and the user declined it. The user's msg 3 also added something new: report code 0's share by month.

So the agent confirmed once, on a treatment that went beyond what the user had said. The finding's claim that awb-clean's rule drove this is contradicted by the agent's own state record and by the scan contents.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-clean/SKILL.md:31 (the rule the finding cites) applies to scan issues, and SKILL.md:33 routes issues the scan missed through the same decision step. But the code-0 row was not a scan issue: foundation/scans/yellow_trips.json S1-S13 contains no payment_type entry. In the same turn, the agent's state record lists only two pending cleaning decisions: relay/agent-002.jsonl, `awb.py state issues --add "Cleaning of yellow_trips awaits two user decisions: very high base fares ... and 28 positive-fare trips..."`. awb-clean/SKILL.md:29 also shows the release means to record a user decision so it is not asked again. None of this ties the re-confirmation to the release.

verdicts.reasoning:
The run evidence is real. In msg 2 the user said "Investigate payment code 0, but don't treat it alone as proof that a trip is invalid" and set the tip measure as "median tip percentage across all credit-card trips". The reply 2 decision table has a row "Payment code 0 | ... | **Confirm**: count them everywhere except credit-card tipping ... | Also report their recorded tips as a separate figure." The human feedback (pain point 7) and orchestrator-report item 9 both complain about it. Note that the cited ID "taxi-B-15" in feedback/findings.json is about something else (check-draft bullets); the actual evidence is transcript msg 2 against reply 2.

Two things undercut the finding.

1. The awb-clean rule it blames did not drive the question. That rule applies to classifying the scan's in-scope issues. The scan (foundation/scans/yellow_trips.json, relay/agent-002.jsonl) listed S1-S13: negatives, ranges, extremes and text-typed. None of them concerns payment_type. Code 0 appeared only as a null pattern. The agent's own `state issues` note, written in the same turn, says cleaning "awaits two user decisions": the high fares and the 28 negative-charge trips. Code 0 is not on it, so the agent did not treat code 0 as a pending awb-clean decision. Code 0 was later recorded as new issue DQ-013 with "none in the foundation; investigations decide", which is consistent with the user's earlier instruction. The skill never says to re-ask a choice the user has already made. Elsewhere the release discourages confirmation rounds: awb-scope says "Write the records without a separate confirmation round" and "carry settled answers forward".

2. The treatment did not simply follow from the user's principle. The user said only "not invalid" and "credit-card trips". The agent found that code 0 ("Flex Fare") trips have no recorded payment method and that 22% of them show a tip. Because cash tips are not recorded, a recorded tip suggests card payment. So whether code 0 trips, or the ones with tips, belong in card tipping was a real interpretive question. The row also offered a real alternative the user had not addressed: reporting the recorded tips for code 0 separately. The user's answer added a new requirement ("report their share by month") and declined that alternative. Checking a concrete case where the stated rule is ambiguous is what awb-scope's "Follow up before moving on" asks for. It is not a defect.

Cost: none in turns. The row sat in a single table with three decisions the user had to answer anyway, as awb-clean's "ask all of these in one message" directs. At most this was agent phrasing, calling it "Confirm" instead of "I'll apply X; say if you want Y". No release text causes it.
verdicts.release_evidence: The cited rule, awb-clean/SKILL.md:31 ("The user decides every other issue..."), applies to classifying scan issues. Payment code 0 was not a scan issue (taxi-B/project/foundation/scans/yellow_trips.json, issues S1-S13), and the agent's own pending-decision note in relay/agent-002.jsonl lists only the high-fare and negative-charge decisions. Text that works against re-confirmation: awb-scope/SKILL.md:42 ("Write the records without a separate confirmation round") and :25 ("carry settled answers forward"). awb-scope/SKILL.md:27 asks the agent to confirm an answer by restating it as a concrete case, which fits a genuinely ambiguous code-0 case (22% recorded tips, payment method unknown).

consolidated.title: The analysis guide does not say packaged results need an 'answers' declaration
consolidated.description: The ledger storyline needs an 'answers' declaration on every result a package represents, but analysis.md presents 'answers' as optional. The agent had to add it to eight results after the fact.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-26: package-contract 'Ledger storyline' puts findings without answers last and lists them in unlinked_findings; reply 5 log.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and found none. The gap is in how the agent read the documents the release ships. Interactivity, the Codex sandbox, MCP auto-approval, the simulated home folder, the relay and the persona all play no part. The agent's copy of the skills in agent-home/.claude/skills matches the release.

What happened, from primary sources:
1. In reply 3 (relay/agent-003.jsonl, line 95) the agent wrote all the results in one script. It declared `answers` on one primary result per ledger question and gave eight others an empty list: screening-by-rule, volume-by-weekday-hour, volume-by-hour, airport-share, tips-by-hour, top-zones-keeping-high-fares and top-zones-10000-trips (zone-count-check, the eighth, came later). Several of these carry exactly the same `question` text as the result that did declare it.
2. In reply 5 (relay/agent-005.jsonl, line 110) the agent had just read awb-package's package-contract. Before writing any draft, and with no check-draft failure prompting it, it added `answers` to exactly those eight results in a single settings.toml edit. feedback/agent.md section 1 item 5 and agent-notes.md turn 5 say the need was "not obvious up front".

Why the release is the cause:
- The settings template labels the key "optional" and gives one purpose for it: run.py marks the questions answered. One declaration per question already does that, so declaring it on secondary results looks redundant.
- analysis.md says only to declare `answers` "when it answers ledger data questions". Nothing in it says packaging reads each represented result's `answers` to order slides.
- The package contract and the draft checker say a slide whose cited results have no `answers` sorts last and goes into `unlinked_findings`. The checker deliberately does not fall back to the slide's other represented results.
- So the requirement first shows up only at packaging time. Any agent on a normal interactive host that reads "optional" the same way will hit it. Other runs show the same uneven habit: taxi-A and co2-B also left some results without `answers`. They avoided unlinked slides only because their slides also cited a linked result.

Reasons for medium confidence rather than high:
- The finding overstates analysis.md. It is the settings template that says "optional"; analysis.md's wording is conditional. Most of the eight results did answer a ledger question, so a strict reading of analysis.md would already have had the agent declare them. Part of the cause is agent judgment.
- The impact is small. The fix was one edit, and no rerun was needed because `answers` is read from current settings. Left unfixed, the slides would only sort last, with an informational list, or the user could approve a presentation order instead.
- The finding's cited ID is wrong. taxi-B-26 in feedback/findings.json is the cash-tips (Q-006) item. The real support is agent.md item 5 and the reply 5 relay log.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/settings.toml:19 calls the key optional: `answers = ["Q-004"]  # optional: ledger data questions this result answers; run.py marks them answered.` awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md:11 gives the condition ("`answers = ["Q-NNN"]` when it answers ledger data questions") and says nothing about packaging needing it. awb-package/references/package-contract.md:33: slides that answer no ledger question go last and are listed in `unlinked_findings`. awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:2370-2371: there is no fallback from a slide's other represented results. awb-package/SKILL.md:37: the storyline is derived from each represented result's recorded settings `answers` only at packaging time.

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding says analysis.md presents `answers` as optional. It does not. The analysis guide makes it conditional: "`answers = ["Q-NNN"]` when it answers ledger data questions" (analysis.md:11). Only the commented settings.toml template uses the word "optional".

The run evidence shows the agent did not follow that instruction, rather than being misled by the guide. In turn 3 (relay/agent-003.jsonl, the script that generates settings.toml), the agent gave five results the exact ledger question text as their `question`, but set `answers` on only one result per question:
- screening-by-rule (Q4)
- volume-by-weekday-hour (Q1)
- airport-share (Q2)
- tips-by-hour (Q3)
- volume-by-hour (Q1)

Under the guide's wording, each of these answers a ledger data question, so each should have declared `answers`.

The other three results it linked later are follow-up checks the user requested: top-zones-keeping-high-fares, top-zones-10000-trips and zone-count-check. For results like these, the package contract already has a designed outcome:
- Slides that answer no ledger question go last.
- They are listed in `unlinked_findings`, which helpers.md:29 calls "informational".
- A user-approved `presentation_order` overrides the order completely.

So "the ledger storyline needs an answers declaration on every result" overstates the contract. Without `answers`, a slide is ordered last; nothing fails.

The late linking also cost almost nothing, and the release supports it:
- The agent read package-contract.md "Ledger storyline" and awb-package SKILL.md:37, which tells it to read each represented result's `answers`.
- It then added the eight declarations with one script, before drafting (agent-005.jsonl lines 105-112).
- No check-draft failure was involved. `stale` reported 0, because the guide says declaring or changing `answers` "computes nothing and makes no result stale" (analysis.md:17).
- The user never saw it.

The finding's evidence citation is also mislabelled. findings.json taxi-B-26 is about cash tips; the matching entry is taxi-B-14.

One small documentation improvement remains possible: analysis.md could mention that packages use `answers` to order slides. But the cause the finding gives, that analysis.md calls `answers` optional, is contradicted by the shipped text. The friction came from the agent leaving out an instruction it had already read.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md:11 makes the declaration conditional ("`answers = ["Q-NNN"]` when it answers ledger data questions"), which contradicts the "optional" claim; analysis.md:17 says late declaration computes nothing and stales nothing. awb-package/references/helpers.md:29 says `unlinked_findings` "is informational", and package-contract.md:33 puts unlinked slides last by design. awb-package/SKILL.md:37 points the agent to `answers` at package time. Only awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/settings.toml:19 says "optional". Run: taxi-B/relay/agent-003.jsonl (turn 3 settings script) set `answers` = [] on five results whose question text equals the ledger question; agent-005.jsonl lines 105-112 added all eight in one edit before drafting, with stale = 0.

consolidated.title: A failed publish leaves a partial directory, and the output does not say so
consolidated.description: A failed publish left a p1.partial directory. The command output does not say it must be removed before retrying; only references/landing.md says so.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-31: ChecksFailed key:trip_id in agent-002, then a manual rm -rf of p1.partial; landing.md.

verdicts.reasoning:
Nothing about how the simulation was run explains this. In taxi-B, relay/agent-002.jsonl (line 67) shows the agent's own CLI call `awb.py publish yellow_trips p1` failing. Its regex took the month from the directory name rather than the file name, so trip_id repeated, and the declared check `key:trip_id` refused the publication. The refusal JSON was `{"published": false, "error": "ChecksFailed: ...", "failed_checks": [...], "partial": "data/parquet/yellow_trips/p1.partial"}`. It gives the path and nothing else. The agent's next call (line 71) ran `rm -rf .../p1.partial` and then republished. Its feedback (agent.md section 3, agent-notes.md turn 2) says the output named the directory but did not say whether a rerun cleans it up.

The release decides this behaviour, not the harness:
- The CLI prints only the partial path when it refuses.
- `publish()` refuses any later run whose partial destination already exists (`_refuse_existing(final, partial)`). A plain retry would therefore fail with `FileExistsError` and still give no next step.
- The MCP `data` tool routes `publish` to the same CLI, so using the CLI instead of MCP changed nothing.
- The project copies of data.md and landing.py are byte-identical to the release.

On guidance, the workbench guide's publish section (data.md:39) says a failing check refuses publication but never mentions the partial directory or the retry refusal. `publish --help` says only "the partial directory left behind". The one place that says to clear it before retrying is landing.md:47. data.md:5 tells readers to open landing.md only when writing `fetch`/`convert` callables, archives or spreadsheets, so someone using the CLI is never sent there.

I checked each harness cause and none applies:
- **Non-interactive run or auto-approval:** the `rm -rf` was auto-approved by a config rule. On an interactive host it would only prompt the user, which makes the friction more visible, not less.
- **Sandbox or simulated home:** no involvement.
- **Relay:** no relay text is involved; the refusal output above came from the command itself.
- **Persona front-loading:** the human was Codex and was not involved in this step.

The failure that triggered the partial was a real agent bug, the kind any user could hit.

Limits:
- **Severity:** the impact really is minor. The agent recovered in one step and the run lost nothing.
- **Bad citation:** the finding cites the wrong evidence ID. taxi-B-31 is the Codex meta-line harness finding; the matching entry in feedback/findings.json is taxi-B-19. The underlying evidence is still present and supports the claim.
- **Wording:** "does not say it must be removed" is accurate, but `--help` does mention the leftover directory.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/awb_landing.py:1117-1119 (on refusal the CLI prints only "partial": <path>); awb-init/assets/awb_landing.py:571-572 (`_refuse_existing(final, partial)` refuses a retry while p1.partial exists); awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md:39 (publish section never mentions the partial directory or the retry refusal) and :5 (sends readers to landing.md only to write callables, archives or spreadsheets); awb-init/references/landing.md:47 (the only place that says to clear it before retrying)

verdicts.reasoning:
The release causes this. The cited run evidence is real, but it carries the wrong ID: in taxi-B/feedback/findings.json the matching finding is taxi-B-19. taxi-B-31 is an unrelated harness finding about a Codex meta-line in user message 1.

What the run shows: in relay/agent-002.jsonl the first `awb.py publish yellow_trips p1` failed with output `{"published": false, "error": "ChecksFailed: Declared checks failed: key:trip_id (2964624 of 6041527 rows repeat a key)", "failed_checks": [...], "partial": "data/parquet/yellow_trips/p1.partial"}`. The agent's next command began `rm -rf data/parquet/yellow_trips/p1.partial && ...` and then republished. Its notes (feedback/agent-notes.md:18, feedback/agent.md:43) say the output named the directory but did not say whether a rerun cleans it up.

What the release does:
- publish() calls `_refuse_existing(final, partial)` (awb_landing.py:571-573), so retrying with the same ID is refused until the .partial directory is removed.
- On failure the CLI prints only the partial path, with no next step (awb_landing.py:1117-1119).
- The `publish --help` epilog, which the agent read, says only "and the partial directory left behind" (awb_landing.py:1031-1033).
- The guide the agent followed for publishing, workbench-guides/data.md:39, says only that a failing check refuses publication and that failed_checks names it. It never mentions the partial directory.
- The only instruction, "A failure leaves an unpublished partial directory; resolve it deliberately before retrying", is in awb-init/references/landing.md:47. data.md:5 tells readers to open landing.md only when writing fetch or convert callables, landing archives or spreadsheets, or handling read refusals, so the CLI path never sends anyone there.

The finding is accurate as stated, and it would happen on any host. Impact is small. A blind retry would fail with a FileExistsError naming the .partial path, which is fairly self-explanatory. In this run the agent cleaned up before retrying, so it lost no attempts. The real cost was uncertainty plus an unguided rm -rf. That fits the "minor" severity. I gave medium rather than high confidence because the release does name the leftover directory, and the friction stayed small.

consolidated.title: check-draft does not warn when methodology cites a result the manifest does not represent
consolidated.description: After the export wrapper dropped two results, check-draft still passed while methodology cited record-reconciliation. The agent caught the gap only by inspecting the manifest.
consolidated.evidence: taxi-B-33: reply 6.

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding says check-draft passed while methodology cited a result the manifest did not hold. The transcript does not show that, and a reproduction contradicts it.

1. check-draft never ran against the 15-result manifest. In relay/agent-006.jsonl, step 92 ran the agent's own wrapper `sh ../agent-home/scratch/awb-export-board.sh --result record-reconciliation --result newark-pickup-durations`. The wrapper had no "$@", so the extra arguments were dropped. The export output the agent piped through printed `True [] {...} 15`, and that count of 15 is what alerted it. At step 97 it checked manifest.json and found 15 results, and at step 99 it wrote "The script ignored the extra arguments".
